entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 106 · Thursday, the Twenty-Second of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the pennant races rest.

1 days until the opening game of the 122nd World's Series — Misiorowski against Rasmussen, the Rays at Milwaukee, eight o'clock Friday evening (Friday, the 23rd of October, 2026).

News Around the League

THE TRIBUNAL DESK: THE MECHANICAL ARBITER COMES TO ITS FIRST WORLD'S SERIES — AND THE TWO CLUBS THAT QUESTION EVERYTHING ELSE IN BASEBALL WILL NOT QUESTION THE UMPIRE, SAVE FROM BEHIND THE PLATE, WHERE DÍAZ HAS LET NINE-AND-FIFTY BAD CALLS GO BY WITHOUT A WORD

The automated ball-strike challenge — the tap of the helmet that summons the machine to overrule the man — finished its first season this year, and Friday it plays its first World's Series. The delicious part is who brings it there. Milwaukee and Tampa Bay are the two most relentlessly analytical operations in the game, clubs that will interrogate any ledger for the thinnest edge, and both have arrived at the same conclusion about the new privilege: hoard it, and spend it through the catcher. Batting, the two clubs together have claimed just 4 of the 43 overturns October offered them; fielding, 21 of 40. Every one of the seven batting challenges between them belongs to Milwaukee — Tampa Bay's hitters have not tapped a helmet all fall.3

The abstention runs deeper than strategy; in two cases it approaches principle. Of the 139 batters this year who saw at least 25 wrongly called pitches with a challenge still in hand, 137 protested at least once. The two holdouts will both dress for the Series: Milwaukee's Andrew Vaughn, who let 36 such calls pass, and Tampa Bay's Yandy Díaz, who let a scarcely believable 59 go unprotested. Díaz explained himself to the Tampa Bay Times back in June: "When I go to home plate, I need a hit, not a challenge. Maybe in the World Series sometime, but now, no."3 It is the World Series now. His manager, Kevin Cash, calls the economy a habit rather than a commandment: "If we get the lead after the sixth or seventh inning, we are reminding guys to save them for the catcher... It's got to be kind of a run-scoring, game-changing at-bat."3

Milwaukee's reticence has an enforcement arm. The rookie outfielder Luis Lara, wrong on five of his seven tries, was relieved of the franchise entirely. "We took him offline," the manager Pat Murphy said late in the season. "He can't get any worse. We've got a reverse magnet so if his hand goes near his head, it goes away."3

Where the two clubs do spend, they collect. Tampa Bay and Milwaukee stand first and second in challenge value gained on the fielding side this postseason, and the catchers are the paymasters: William Contreras leads all of October with 12 overturns, while Liam Hicks owns three of the seven most consequential challenge moments of the month — among them the call in the sixth game of the American round that turned a would-be full count with two aboard into an inning-ending strikeout.3 So the question the Series will answer is not whether the machine matters but who dares consult it: if a championship game ends on a pitch nobody challenges, the sport will hear about it all winter.

THE LARCENY DESK: ONE-AND-TWENTY BASES ALREADY STOLEN THIS OCTOBER AND NOT A MAN THROWN OUT ON THE TAMPA SIDE — THE FASTEST CLUB IN BASEBALL MEETS THE SECOND-BOLTINGEST, AND ONLY ONE PENNANT WINNER OF THE WHOLE WILD CARD ERA EVER RAN MORE

If the arms decide nothing, the legs may decide everything. Milwaukee was the fastest club in baseball this season — first in average sprint speed and first in runs clocked at the elite 30-feet-per-second gait the measuring men call a bolt — and Tampa Bay, slower only on average, banked the second-most bolts in the game. The running followed the speed: 164 stolen bases for the Rays, tied for second in the majors, and 162 for the Brewers, fifth. Only one pennant winner of the entire Wild Card era, the 2023 Arizonans with 166, ever stole more in a regular season than either of these clubs, and this is just the fourth Series since 1969 to pair two of the year's five busiest thieving outfits. The last such meeting, Rays and Phillies in 2008, produced 14 steals in a five-game Series — the most of this century — and neither of these clubs has shown any inclination to let that record rest. Tampa Bay has stolen 11 bases in 11 tries across nine playoff games; Milwaukee is 10 for 12 in eight.4

The Tampa running trade is a one-man syndicate with branch offices. Chandler Simpson has never hit a home run in his major-league life and rarely accepts a walk, yet batted .306, led all of baseball with 42 infield hits, led the American League with 46 steals, and has added three more this October; behind him Taylor Walls and Cedric Mullins stole 21 apiece, Richie Palacios and Jonny DeLuca 17 each. Milwaukee counters with the committee: seven Brewers stole at least 11 bases, David Hamilton taking 30 in only 121 games — and 3 for 3 this October — while the rookie shortstop Cooper Pratt lifted 19 after a June debut and Jackson Chourio owns three straight seasons of 20 or more.4

Here is the asymmetry that may tilt the footrace: Milwaukee allowed the second-fewest steals in baseball this year, 71, while Tampa Bay surrendered the sixth-most, 131. The catchers' ledgers look lopsided — Contreras threw out 34 percent of basestealers to Hicks' 15.9 — though the measuring men rate their arms nearer even given what each was asked to stop; the true gap lives on the mound, where Milwaukee's pitchers rank among the game's best at holding runners and Tampa Bay's among its worst.4 The opening game states the whole thesis in miniature: Jacob Misiorowski, nearly impossible to run on, against Drew Rasmussen, on whom only three pitchers in baseball allowed more steals than his 23 — though Rasmussen has kept the question moot this October by the simple expedient of allowing almost nobody aboard: 13 hits and 3 walks in 21 innings, a 1.29 figure. Runners cannot steal what they cannot reach.4

THE REMEMBRANCE DESK: 'WHEREVER WE GATHER, WE KNOW HE'S RIGHT HERE CHEERING ALONGSIDE US' — ON THE EVE OF MILWAUKEE'S FIRST WORLD'S SERIES SINCE 1982, THE UECKER FAMILY WRITES A LETTER TO THE CITY

The most affecting dispatch of the idle day carried no statistics at all. On the eve of Milwaukee's first World's Series in 44 years, the family of Bob Uecker — the voice bound up with the Brewers beyond any untangling — addressed an open letter to the city, and it reads less like a press notice than like something passed across a kitchen table. "Some moments are worth waiting for," it begins, and arrives soon enough at the ache inside the celebration: "We are filled with elation and pride, but also longing. A wish that Bob was here to see it, too."5

The family writes that Milwaukee, the Brewers, and the fans "meant everything to Bob," and offers this certainty in place of his voice: "Wherever we gather — in a packed stadium, a neighborhood bar, or a living room with the radio turned all the way up — we know he's right here cheering alongside us." To the players: "Bob would have been so incredibly proud of what you've accomplished." There are thanks besides for the Attanasio family and Pat Murphy, for the broadcast booth that carries his tradition forward, and for the fans who have kept his spirit alive "through a laugh, a story, a cold beer, or a favorite call." The letter closes at full volume: "Milwaukee, let's get loud, let's do this together, let's win OUR way!"5

The Herald adds only this: a ballclub is finally a collection of the people who cared about it longest, and no franchise ever had a truer voice than the one Milwaukee will be listening for between the cheers on Friday night.

THE LONG ROAD DESK: THE SCOUT WENT TO TIJUANA FOR AROZARENA, WHO NEVER APPEARED — ELEVEN YEARS, EIGHT FARM CLUBS AND ONE ABANDONED CATCHING EXPERIMENT LATER, THE SHORTSTOP HE FOUND INSTEAD BATS IN THE MIDDLE OF A PENNANT WINNER

Every World's Series roster hides one story that explains the whole franchise, and Tampa Bay's is Jonathan Aranda's. In 2015 the club's international scouting director, Carlos Rodriguez, traveled to Tijuana to evaluate a Cuban outfielder named Randy Arozarena — whom the Rays could not then have afforded to sign in any case — and Arozarena never showed up for the workout. Rodriguez, holding to a scout's creed that "you're always dangerous at the ballpark," asked to see the academy's younger players so the trip would not be wasted, and came away intrigued by a 17-year-old shortstop of 160 pounds. The Rays signed him for $130,000 on July 2, 2015.6

What followed is the less accidental half of the story: eleven years of stubborn institutional faith. Aranda played for eight clubs in the Tampa Bay system, some at levels that no longer exist, and was bounced around the infield for a decade — there were men in the organization who doubted he would ever reach Double-A, and after the lost season of 2020 the club floated the idea of making him a catcher. He answered with his bat instead, hitting .330 with a .418 on-base figure and .543 slugging at Double-A Montgomery in 2021 without ever starting a game behind the plate. He battered Triple-A pitching at a .315 clip across three seasons while batting just .222 in scattered major-league chances, and the manager Kevin Cash kept repeating the creed of the patient: too good at Durham not to hit in the majors eventually.6

Eventually arrived this year. Healthy at last, Aranda started 148 games — only Junior Caminero and Yandy Díaz answered the bell more often — and batted .274 with a .792 on-base-plus-slugging, his left-handed swing wedged between Díaz and Caminero precisely so that no manager can cheaply spend a right-handed reliever on the pair of them. He is now the longest-tenured player in the organization. "Player development success story and scouting success story — both of those," says Jeff McLerran, the club's senior director of baseball development, recalling the scouts' promise down all those years: "This guy will hit. I promise you, this guy will hit."6 He did. Friday the promise reports to the World's Series.

One day. The ledgers stand exactly as the pennant rounds left them — Milwaukee four games to one over Los Angeles, Tampa Bay four to two over Cleveland, and the Series line a pair of unblemished zeros waiting for Friday.1 The particulars hold as this paper has printed them all week: the first two games at Milwaukee, Friday the 23rd and Saturday the 24th at eight o'clock Eastern, the argument removing to St. Petersburg on Monday the 26th.2 Milwaukee hands the opener to Jacob Misiorowski, whose 1.80 earned-run average, 252 strikeouts and 0.80 walks-and-hits figure led the league this season, and Tampa Bay is expected to answer with Drew Rasmussen, unbeaten in 15 starts since the All-Star interval.8 The rosters come due Friday morning ahead of the first game, and with them the last suspense the off-days can offer.7 Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 105 · Wednesday, the Twenty-First of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the pennant races rest.

2 days until the first game of the 122nd World's Series — the Rays at the Brewers, eight o'clock Friday evening at Milwaukee (Friday, the 23rd of October, 2026).

News Around the League

THE ALIGNMENT DESK: WINNING IN SIX PAYS ITS DIVIDEND IN REST — RASMUSSEN POINTED TOWARD A THIRD STRAIGHT FIRST GAME, PERALTA'S DAY THE ONE RIDDLE LEFT ON THE TAMPA SLATE, AND EVERY ARM OF BOTH STAFFS REPORTS FRESH FOR FRIDAY

Yesterday's number set out how fat with rest Milwaukee would come to the opener — a full week off since its sweep of the Dodgers concluded last Thursday, its ace eleven days between hostile innings. The fuller ledger shows Tampa Bay scarcely behind. By settling the pennant in six games the Rays were spared the all-hands seventh that empties a pitching staff, and bought themselves an extra day besides.3

Drew Rasmussen last worked Sunday evening in Cleveland, which leaves him his accustomed four days to Friday night; he opened the division round and the pennant round alike, and nothing in the club's conduct suggests the World's Series will begin any differently. Asked after Monday's clinching for his program, the right-hander offered a working man's itinerary: "Throw a bullpen and figure out what game I get to start."3 The genuine riddle is Freddy Peralta, most valuable man of the American round. Four days' rest would serve him perfectly well for Saturday's second game — in Milwaukee, against the club that raised him — but the Rays have made a quiet habit this month of starting him under their own roof, and a third-game assignment Monday at St. Petersburg would still permit him two starts should the argument run long. "We'll think about that in a few days," said the president of baseball operations, Erik Neander.3

The bookkeeping behind them is equally kind. Bryan Baker, who has finished every one of Tampa Bay's seven October victories with seven scoreless innings and worked three straight nights to close out Cleveland, now collects a holiday; Griffin Jax has not pitched since Thursday and Nick Martinez since Friday, so both report rested for the early-series bullpen errands the Rays favor before the rotation comes back around.34 Milwaukee's late innings are no less fortified: its relief corps stands 7 wins against 1 defeat with a 1.33 figure this postseason — every decision in the club's eight games has belonged to the bullpen — and Trevor Megill, Aaron Ashby and DL Hall have thrown 23 1/3 scoreless innings between them while holding batters to a .096 average.4 Two staffs, fully wound. Friday releases the spring.

THE INFIRMARY DESK: THREE-AND-TWENTY LIVE PITCHES AFTER FOUR SILENT MONTHS — WOODRUFF PRESSES HIS CLAIM ON A ROSTER DUE FRIDAY MORNING, WHILE ACROSS THE FIELD McCLANAHAN'S OCTOBER IS OVER BEFORE IT BEGAN

Brandon Woodruff, the longest-tenured man on the Milwaukee roll, threw 23 live pitches at American Family Field on Tuesday to the first string itself — Jackson Chourio, Brice Turang, William Contreras and Christian Yelich, with Jake Bauers stepping in when the count wanted filling — and sat at 90 to 92 miles the hour, facing hitters for the first time in nearly four months.5 He has not pitched in a game since the 4th of July, when the surgically repaired shoulder complained a second time and season-ending surgery was fixed for August. Then the unexpected: the shoulder healed, the surgeon blessed a comeback, and five weeks of throwing carried him to bullpen mounds between division-round games and again at Los Angeles during the pennant round. The schedule cooperated at every step, and now the last door stands ajar: the Series roster is due Friday morning.5

The decision is thornier than sentiment. By the league's rules a man injured during a postseason series may be replaced only for "an acute, non-chronic injury or ailment," as a report from Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic set out Tuesday — and whether a fresh complaint from a twice-angry shoulder would qualify is exactly the apprehension in Milwaukee's councils. A wrong guess could leave the club a man short for the length of the Series. "Still working through our meetings," said the president of baseball operations, Matt Arnold.5 The pitcher himself pleads his case and grants the other side of it in the same breath: "I'm not going to be mad either way... All I could do was put myself in a position to be an option." And the larger ledger, in his own words: "Obviously, the competitor in me wants to be suited up for our first World Series in 44 years... This city is buzzing, man. This is about this organization, this city, and trying to win its first World Series."5

Tampa Bay's infirmary page is shorter and sadder: Shane McClanahan is ruled out for the postseason entirely, though the club expects him ready when spring comes. Otherwise both wards stand empty — a Series between the two best records in baseball, played at something close to full strength.4

THE GAUNTLET DESK: CLEVELAND DREW MILWAUKEE A MAP — FASTBALLS UPSTAIRS FOR CAMINERO, ELEVEN STRIKEOUTS IN FIVE GAMES — BUT THE MOST HEATER-PROUD ROTATION THE INSTRUMENTS HAVE EVER COUNTED MUST TEST IT AGAINST THE MAN WHO SLUGGED .882 ON HIGH FIRE ALL SUMMER

The central duel of this World's Series was drafted in the one just ended. Cleveland's pitchers attacked the Rays with four-seam fastballs 37.8 percent of the time in the pennant round, and fed Junior Caminero in particular a diet of them pitched higher than in any month of his career. For five games it worked handsomely: 4 hits in 20 trips with 11 strikeouts — he had never before struck out more than 8 in any five-game span — and of 26 four-seamers shown him out of the strike zone he chased fully half, at an average height of 3.70 feet off the ground. His swing-and-miss rate on pitches outside the zone, 37.5 percent across the season, has jumped to 53.5 this October.6 The answer, when it came, rang off the left-field foul pole in Game 6 and carried the Rays to the Series, as yesterday's number told at length.

Here is the paradox Milwaukee must now price: by the season's full ledger the high fastball is precisely the pitch Caminero punishes best. His flat, level stroke and the speed of his bat keep him on plane with elevated heat; against four-seamers at the belt or above he hit .368 and slugged .882, damage exceeded by one man in baseball, and his .641 slugging against the pitch overall stood among the ten best in the game.6 The Guardians bet that October nerves would beat the summer's arithmetic, and for five games they were right.

And no club is better armed to re-run the experiment — or more committed by temperament. Milwaukee's starters threw 41 percent four-seamers this season, the highest allotment in the majors (Tampa Bay's own starters, by instructive contrast, threw fewer than 25), and struck out more batters with the pitch than any rotation in the whole of the pitch-tracking record, which reaches back to 2008 — nearly a hundred clear of the next club. Jacob Misiorowski alone threw the four-seamer 63 percent of the time at an average of 100.6 miles the hour, and 166 of his 252 strikeouts finished on it.7 The club's pitching instructor, Chris Hook, states the doctrine without embroidery: "It's either the pitcher's in charge, or the hitter's in charge... 'Hey man, I'm going to bully you.' That's that edge we're looking for."7 High fire against the game's best high-fire hitter, with the championship of the world on the table: the Series could be decided a letter's width above the strike zone.

THE CHALK DESK: NOT ONE UPSET ALL OCTOBER — THE BETTER RECORD HAS CARRIED EVERY SERIES OF THE BRACKET, AND A MILWAUKEE TITLE WOULD CLOSE A POSTSEASON TO FORM AS NO AMERICAN SPORT HAS MANAGED UNDER ITS PRESENT RULES

The bracket has behaved all month with a discipline October rarely shows. Every series so far has gone to the club with the better regular-season record; the one lower seed to advance — the sixth-seeded White Sox over the third-seeded Astros in the wild-card round — in fact owned the better ledger, 84 wins against 81. The final it has produced, each league's best record with 103 and 98 wins respectively, is only the sixth such meeting of the Wild Card era, which dates from 1995.8

The wider books make the run rarer still. Since the four major American leagues settled into their present playoff shapes — this game in 2022, the basketball league in 2021, the football league in 2020, the hockey league in 2014 — not one postseason among them has gone entirely to the better record. Some underdog always collects: a year ago it was the Dodgers, with one win fewer, over Toronto in the Series.8 Should Milwaukee finish what its 103 wins began, the 2026 bracket would be the first in any of the four sports to run true from first pitch to last.

The Herald, which has spent a full summer arguing that 162 games constitute the sounder tribunal, declines to call this dullness. When the best teams of April through September are also the last two standing in October, the proper word is not chalk but justice — and the two clubs in question, it happens, are the two that have never once been champion. Form and novelty, for one week at least, pull the same oar.

THE TIMELESS TICKET DESK: A THOUSAND DOLLARS IN 2015 BOUGHT 'THE BEST AVAILABLE SEAT' AT ANY GAME TO COME — SEVERAL HUNDRED OF THE FAITHFUL CALLED THE NOTE FOR THE SERIES, WERE SHOWN THE FOURTH DECK, AND HAVE NOW BEEN MADE WHOLE

In 2015, with the club going nowhere in particular, Milwaukee sold a promotion called the Timeless Ticket: one thousand dollars for admission to any single game in all the future, redeemable per the offer's own language "for the best available seat locations, subject to ticket availability," with the right to buy three further seats at retail alongside. The purest buyers were buying exactly one thing — this week. Now the Series has come to Milwaukee for the first time since 1982, several hundred holders have presented their notes, and the redemption did not match the prospectus: a form offering only 400-level perches or standing room, with no saying even which game.9

Danny Fochesato of Milwaukee, who bought his on his 27th birthday against precisely this occasion, recalls the selling pitch — priority just behind the season-ticket holders, "anything the season-ticket holders don't have, you'll have dibs at it for the World Series" — and notes that in 2018, when the club came within a game of the Series, the same ticket would have fetched him seats in the 100 level behind the plate. This time he bargained his way to three fourth-deck seats for Saturday and one lower seat in the right-field corner for Friday, then stood in the public sale and watched better locations offered to all comers.9 "I immediately was like, 'No, that's bogus,'" he said, and this paper, whose sympathies in any contest between the ledger and the bleacherite are a matter of record, finds the verdict sound: a promise sold to the faithful in 2015 ought to trade at full face in 2026.

To the club's credit, the business president Rick Schlesinger conceded the error in plain words — "we did not live up to the spirit of the program" — and the amends go past apology: every holder who applied by the deadline keeps the World's Series tickets and retains the Timeless Ticket itself, to be redeemed for another game in any season to come.9 The note, in other words, pays out twice. The Herald records the resolution with approval and a moral: never sell the future short to the people who believed in it earliest.

Two idle days stand between the pennants and the proof, and the paper intends to spend them exactly as the clubs will: studying the other fellow. The particulars hold as published — Friday the 23rd and Saturday the 24th at Milwaukee, eight o'clock Eastern both evenings, before the argument removes to St. Petersburg on Monday the 26th.2 The rosters are due Friday morning, the rotations remain officially unspoken, and somewhere in Milwaukee a man with a thousand-dollar ticket eleven years old is deciding what to wear. Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: EIGHTEEN YEARS TO THE VERY NIGHT AFTER IWAMURA LEAPT, THE DOME ROARS AGAIN — CAMINERO RINGS THE FOUL POLE AT A WALKING PACE, DÍAZ PAYS HIS GUARANTEE IN FULL, AND THE RAYS TAKE THE AMERICAN PENNANT FOUR GAMES TO TWO: RAYS 7, GUARDIANS 3
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 104 · Tuesday, the Twentieth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 1 contest from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

EIGHTEEN YEARS TO THE VERY NIGHT AFTER IWAMURA LEAPT, THE DOME ROARS AGAIN — CAMINERO RINGS THE FOUL POLE AT A WALKING PACE, DÍAZ PAYS HIS GUARANTEE IN FULL, AND THE RAYS TAKE THE AMERICAN PENNANT FOUR GAMES TO TWO: RAYS 7, GUARDIANS 3

Freddy Peralta carries one-run ball into the sixth and is proclaimed the most valuable man of the round; Richie Palacios, helpless against left-handers all season, wrings a two-run double from one anyway and howls at his own dugout; Junior Caminero's first postseason home run clangs off the left-field pole and is toured in 38.66 seconds, the second-slowest lap the measuring instruments have ever recorded — behind his own; Yandy Díaz closes the account at 111.9 miles the hour one night after declaring it closed; and the first pennant ever clinched on Tropicana Field's own carpet sends Tampa Bay to a World's Series that must crown a first-time champion

Eighteen years ago to the very night — the nineteenth of October, 2008 — Akinori Iwamura gathered a last grounder and leapt off second base beneath Tropicana Field's roof, and 40,473 watched the Rays claim their first pennant. On Monday, the nineteenth of October, 2026, before a sellout of 40,230 under the same roof, Bryan Baker spun a two-strike changeup, Chase DeLauter lifted it foul by the visitors' dugout, Liam Hicks squeezed it, and Baker flung his glove toward the catwalks: Rays 7, Guardians 3, and the American pennant settled four games to two.7 The evening was thick with its own history — B.J. Upton of the worst-to-first 2008 nine threw the ceremonial first pitch, and Tyler Glasnow and Randy Arozarena of the 2020 champions sat in the stands as paying witnesses — and it minted some besides: the 2020 flag having been clinched on neutral ground at San Diego, this was the first pennant ever won upon the Trop's own carpet, a vacancy this paper noted only yesterday morning.73

The contest itself followed the shape the ledgers promised. Cleveland, its rotation spent, stitched the night from eight pitchers beginning with Shawn Armstrong, who lasted the single inning and took the defeat; Tampa Bay handed the ball to Freddy Peralta, who gave them 5 1/3 innings of one-run ball on 84 pitches, 33 of them at 97 miles the hour or better — a career high for the 30-year-old.4 The first blow fell in the second, and it belonged to the unlikeliest man in the order: Richie Palacios, whom left-handers held to a .158 average this season, fought off Tim Herrin pitch after pitch and then lined a double into the right-center gap, his helmet tumbling behind him as Chandler Simpson and Victor Mesa Jr. crossed, and howled at his own dugout from second base.3 Jonny DeLuca's sacrifice fly made it three in the third, and Nathaniel Lowe's single off Peralta in the sixth — Cleveland's lone answer for seven innings — only trimmed the margin. Peralta's account for the round: three appearances, 12 innings, one earned run, an 0.75 average, and the Most Valuable laurels, in company with Matt Garza of 2008 and Arozarena of 2020 among Rays so honored.4

Then came the seventh, and the moment the month had been withholding. Junior Caminero, 42 home runs in the regular season and none in 36 postseason trips to the plate, caught Cade Smith's offering and sent it soaring down the left field line until it clanged off the foul pole — a two-run blow, Hicks scoring ahead of him, and the beginning of the slowest victory lap of the autumn. He stopped at the first-base coach's box and beat his chest. He skipped from first to second. He cupped a hand to his ear from second to third. And at the plate he turned to Arozarena, seated just behind home, crossed his arms in the elder showman's own defiant pose, and stepped on the dish: 38.66 seconds in all, the second-slowest uninterrupted tour the measuring instruments have recorded since 2015 — second only to a 40.65-second lap of Caminero's own, taken in September. "He called it," said the 23-year-old, reporting that Arozarena had demanded the home run from the stands before the at-bat began.5 Even Kevin Cash, the most composed man in the building by profession, threw both arms in the air and screamed.5

Cleveland loaded the eighth and pressed two runs across — both forced home, Patrick Bailey walking with the bases full and Angel Martínez struck by a pitch — and for a moment the thing tightened to 5-3. The answer required one swing. Yandy Díaz, who had stood before the writers Sunday night and guaranteed this very result — a proclamation this paper carried in yesterday's number — met Hunter Gaddis's changeup and sent it 416 feet into the left-field seats at 111.9 miles the hour, the second-hardest-struck postseason home run by any Ray in the instruments' ledger, Taylor Walls scoring ahead of him. He flexed the famous right arm, formed a heart with his hands at the plate, and was dragged back out of the dugout by Caminero for a curtain call as the chant of his name came down from the seats. The man Cleveland itself signed off the amateur market in 2013, who hit one home run in 88 games for them before the trade that remade him, had closed his old club's season personally. "I'm really glad he backed it up, that's for sure," said Cash. Asked about Milwaukee, Díaz consulted the same bank book: "It's going to be a great series, but we're winning."6

For the beaten there was no alibi and none sought. "We didn't beat ourselves, we got beat," said Steven Kwan. "They played defense better than us, they hit better than us, they pitched better than us. As a competitor, you can live with that."3 The Cleveland drought, the game's longest sorrow, now stretches into its 78th year — no title since 1948, though four World's Series and seven American pennant rounds have come and gone since — and the young architecture of this club, DeLauter and Travis Bazzana at the bat and Gavin Williams, Parker Messick and Cade Smith on the hill, is the consolation the coming weeks will have to serve.3 The victors fly north. The 122nd World's Series — guaranteed a first-time champion, as neither finalist has ever won one — opens Friday night at Milwaukee, and the particulars are set out at the Series Desk below.

News Around the League

THE SERIES DESK: ONE HUNDRED THREE WINS AGAINST EIGHT-AND-NINETY, THE TOP SEED OF EACH LEAGUE AND NEITHER WITH A TITLE TO ITS NAME — THE 122ND WORLD'S SERIES OPENS FRIDAY AT MILWAUKEE, RASMUSSEN RECKONED LIKELY AGAINST MISIOROWSKI

The bracket's long arithmetic has produced the rarest of finals: the best record in each league, and not a championship between them. Milwaukee, 103 victories and a franchise record, hosts Tampa Bay, 98 victories and the American League's best, beginning Friday night at eight o'clock Eastern at American Family Field; the second game follows Saturday at the same hour, and the argument removes to the Gulf shore dome Monday the 26th and Tuesday the 27th.29 Five franchises have never won the World's Series — these two, the Mariners, the Padres and the Rockies — so whatever else October does, it will strike one name from that list by month's end.9

The pitching question has a probable answer and a flamethrowing certainty. Tampa Bay has announced nothing, but the wire reckons Drew Rasmussen — 11-0 with a 1.73 earned-run average in 15 starts since the All-Star interlude, and the first-game man in both previous rounds — likely for the opener, on his accustomed rest; he would face the very club that drafted him and dealt him to the Rays five years ago.9 Milwaukee's answer is Jacob Misiorowski, who led the whole of the major leagues this season in earned-run average at 1.80, in strikeouts with 252, in walks-and-hits per inning at 0.80 and in opponents' batting at .157, and whose first pitch of the division round traveled 104.8 miles the hour — the swiftest delivery of any postseason since the measuring instruments began their count in 2008. The rest ledger is lopsided in the extreme: the Brewers will have sat eight days since their sweep concluded on the 15th, and their ace will have gone eleven full days between hostile innings — idleness that has cut both ways in Octobers past, as this paper's Sunday number set out at length.93

THE HOMECOMING DESK: BOTH MOST-VALUABLE MEN OF THE PENNANT ROUNDS WILL SPEND THE SERIES STARING AT THE CLUB THAT FIRST DRESSED THEM — PERALTA THE EX-BREWER AND BAUERS THE EX-RAY, CLASSMATES OF 2018, EACH DECORATED BY THE OTHER'S ALMA MATER

The Series arrives wrapped in a coincidence no scenarist would dare submit. Freddy Peralta, most valuable man of the American round, broke into the majors in 2018 with Milwaukee and spent eight seasons there — a 3.59 earned-run average, 1,153 strikeouts, two All-Star selections, and the first-game assignment in the Octobers of 2024 and 2025 — before a January trade sent him to the Mets, where the season soured to a 4.99 figure across 22 starts. Dealt again to Tampa Bay at the August deadline, he posted a 3.25 mark over his final ten outings and has spent this month repaying the gamble with interest.84 Jake Bauers, most valuable man of the National round for his part in Milwaukee's sweep of the Dodgers, debuted that same season of 2018 — with the Rays. After years of wandering he settled in Milwaukee in 2024 and produced the season of his life this year, a career-high 26 home runs.8

So each league's October laureate will open the World's Series opposite the club that first dressed him, both members of the class of 2018, each honored in the other's old colors.8 Peralta, for his part, declines to make it a grudge: "Milwaukee is the team and the city that gave me the opportunity to make my dreams come true, and Milwaukee is going to be always in my heart," he said Monday night, trophy in hand. "But it's time now to compete."4

THE APPOINTMENTS DESK: BOONE KEEPS THE BRONX CHAIR FOR A TENTH SEASON, THE ATHLETICS HAND THEIR BASEBALL AFFAIRS TO TAYLOR SMITH, AND BALTIMORE FETCHES JARED BANNER FROM THE CUBS' FRONT OFFICE

The hiring season opened on three fronts Monday. In New York, Aaron Boone will return as manager of the Yankees in 2027 — the final year of his contract and his tenth season at the helm — by the account of a source, the club itself declining comment. The case for retention is in the ledger: 93 wins this season and the top Wild Card post before the Rays swept the division round away, three American East flags and eight postseasons in nine years, and 790 victories in the span — second in all baseball to the Dodgers' 849.1011

Out west, the Athletics engaged Taylor Smith as president of baseball operations, entrusting the new man with a franchise entering its final year of temporary quarters at West Sacramento before the move to Las Vegas in 2028.12 And in Baltimore, the Orioles named Jared Banner, lately of the Cubs' front office, their new general manager, with the portfolio of player development, coaching and performance.13 Three chairs filled in a day; the winter's real bargaining, over the men who play, awaits the Series' last out.

THE PACIFIC DESK: SATO, TRIPLE CROWN MAN OF THE CENTRAL LEAGUE, WILL BE POSTED FOR THE AMERICAN MARKET — HANSHIN CONSENTS TO PART WITH A BAT OF .306, NINE-AND-THIRTY HOME RUNS AND 106 RUNS DRIVEN HOME

The winter market gained its headline lot before the Series has thrown a pitch. The Hanshin Tigers of Japan's professional league announced they will approve the posting of Teruaki Sato, the left-handed-hitting third baseman who won the Central League's Triple Crown this season — a .306 average, 39 home runs and 106 runs batted in — one year after taking the league's Most Valuable award on 40 home runs and a .924 mark of on-base-plus-slugging.14 Once posted, all 30 clubs will have a 45-day window to treat with him; being past 25 years of age he comes unrestricted, unlike the young Sasaki two winters ago, and Hanshin collects a release fee scaled to whatever contract results.14

The scouting ledger reads thus: 27 years old, turning 28 before next season; durable, never fewer than 120 games in any of six seasons; a strikeout rate of 27 percent over the past two years against a 10.3 percent walk rate; a Golden Glove at third base in 2025, with 262 games of outfield work besides should a new employer prefer him elsewhere; a Japan Series championship with Hanshin in 2023 and a quarterfinal run with Samurai Japan in this spring's World Baseball Classic.14 In a free-agent pool reckoned light on bats, the wire already counts the Mets, Yankees, Dodgers and Phillies among the interested — a queue the Herald expects to lengthen the moment the posting is official.14

THE LEDGER DESK: THE QUALIFYING OFFER RISES TO $23.15 MILLION, UP FIVE PERCENT AND A FRACTION ON THE YEAR — THE STANDING PRICE OF A FREE MAN'S YEAR CLIMBS AGAIN, AND THE HERALD NOTES WHO SET IT CLIMBING

The accountants have fixed this winter's qualifying offer — the one-year tender a club must extend to its departing free agent if it wishes draft compensation for losing him — at $23.15 million, a rise of 5.1 percent over last winter's $22,025,000. The figure is struck each year from the mean of the game's 125 richest salaries, and its steady climb is the cleanest instrument in the public ledger for what the top of the labor market actually pays.15

The Herald, whose sympathies on matters of the purse are a matter of record, offers the number without alarm: a market in which the standing price of one year's work rises five percent is not a market in distress, whatever may be pleaded across the bargaining table in the winter ahead. The offers go out in the days after the Series concludes; the men who receive them will have their own arithmetic to do.

The forward ledger grants everyone a breath: three days without baseball, and then the 122nd World's Series — Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, Friday the 23rd and Saturday the 24th at eight o'clock Eastern, the scene shifting to the dome at St. Petersburg Monday the 26th and Tuesday the 27th, with a seventh game possible as late as the 31st should the argument use every page allotted it.2 A first-time champion is now a mathematical certainty, which the Herald counts among the happiest sentences it has printed all year. The paper will spend the interval as the clubs will — sharpening its pencils and studying the other fellow. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: A RUN IN THE FIRST, A RUN IN THE SECOND, A RUN IN THE THIRD, AND SEVEN INNINGS OF RASMUSSEN TO KEEP THEM — TWELVE HITS WITHOUT ONE OVER THE WALL MUFFLE THE FOREST CITY NINE, AND THE RAYS CARRY THE AMERICAN QUESTION HOME STANDING ONE VICTORY FROM THE WORLD'S SERIES: RAYS 3, GUARDIANS 1
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 103 · Monday, the Nineteenth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 1 contest from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

A RUN IN THE FIRST, A RUN IN THE SECOND, A RUN IN THE THIRD, AND SEVEN INNINGS OF RASMUSSEN TO KEEP THEM — TWELVE HITS WITHOUT ONE OVER THE WALL MUFFLE THE FOREST CITY NINE, AND THE RAYS CARRY THE AMERICAN QUESTION HOME STANDING ONE VICTORY FROM THE WORLD'S SERIES: RAYS 3, GUARDIANS 1

Drew Rasmussen holds Cleveland to one run across seven innings on 95 pitches, feeding the left-handed hitters a changeup he did not own a year ago and retiring 14 of 15 men through the middle of the evening; Yandy Díaz opens the proceedings with a double and collects three hits; Jonny DeLuca forces in the first run with a bases-loaded walk that survives Cleveland's appeal to the electronic arbiter, and Jonathan Aranda and Liam Hicks single home the second and third; Steven Kwan throws out one runner at the plate and robs another at the center-field wall in a losing cause; and Bryan Baker closes his sixth spotless errand of the month — the pennant round returns to St. Petersburg with Tampa Bay ahead three games to two

Nobody in a gray uniform struck a ball over a wall at Progressive Field on Sunday night, and nobody needed to. Tampa Bay assembled its three runs the way a clerk assembles a ledger — one entry at a time, each in its proper column — scoring once in each of the first three innings, a thing the franchise had managed in only three previous October contests.5 In the first, Yandy Díaz led off with a double and walked home when Jonny DeLuca, the bases full, declined ball four; Cleveland's catcher Patrick Bailey appealed the call to the league's electronic arbiter, and the machine sided with the walk. In the second, Jonathan Aranda's single to left cashed Ben Williamson; in the third, Liam Hicks dropped a single into center to cash Chandler Simpson. Twelve hits the visitors collected, and only two — doubles by Díaz and Simpson — advanced a man past first base on their own authority; the beaten starter himself certified the method afterward, describing an unselfish nine that shoots the ball through holes rather than swinging for the fences.3 Tyler Wells, who contributed one strikeout to the cause, put it in the house style: "That was Rays baseball at its finest."5

The man guarding the entries was Drew Rasmussen, on the five days' rest this paper noted yesterday he has kept nearly all season: seven innings, four hits, one walk, six strikeouts, 95 pitches. After Chase DeLauter's two-out single in the first he retired nine men running and 14 of the next 15; only six Cleveland balls escaped the infield all evening, a mere three were hard-struck by the measuring instruments' reckoning, and the lone run arrived in the sixth by way of two singles and DeLauter's groundout.4 The quiet work was done by the newest tool in the box — a changeup built only this year, thrown 27 times to Cleveland's left-handed hitters, 28 percent of his pitches and the heaviest he has ever leaned upon it, without surrendering a hit. "It's probably been the single greatest addition I've made to my repertoire in the entirety of my career," said its author; "Three fastballs and a really good changeup," summarized Stephen Vogt, who found no answer to any of the four.4 The October account now reads 21 innings and three runs across three starts: no Tampa Bay pitcher before him had twice gone seven innings allowing one run or none in a postseason, none had strung three quality starts together, and the last man anywhere to bank two such starts before a World's Series was Logan Webb in 2021. Since the All-Star interlude Rasmussen stands 11-0 with a 1.73 earned-run average, 99 strikeouts against 18 walks in 93 2/3 innings, his club winning 14 of those 15 starts — figures that moved Díaz, through the club's interpreter, to a flat verdict: "I really do think he's the best pitcher in MLB."43 Behind him Cam Booser took two outs, Wells one, and Bryan Baker worked a clean ninth for his fifth save — six errands this October, no runs, one hit allowed in the whole of them, company kept only by Jason Motte and Mark Wohlers among pitchers who finished each of their first six postseason appearances.5

The defeat was not for want of gallantry. Steven Kwan, having judged his own second-inning throw insufficient, atoned in the fourth: he gathered Aranda's single in left and cut down Taylor Walls at the plate on one true bounce to Bailey — "off the bat, I thought there was no chance of a play," admitted Kevin Cash — and in the ninth, shifted to center field, he leapt at the wall to strip Victor Mesa Jr. of extra bases. "I was glad to save some runs there, but I left some meat on the bone, I felt like, with that first one," was the Gold Glove man's own accounting. José Ramírez added a barehanded pickup of Simpson's eighth-inning bunt, and Vogt spoke the epitaph: "That game could have looked a lot different without our defense tonight."6 True, and insufficient — for the deeper wound was the start. Parker Messick, moved up a game by the rainout's arithmetic as this paper set out Sunday, lasted two innings, the shortest start of his career, on 57 laboring pitches; his season's account now stands at exactly 200 innings against a previous professional high of 138 1/3, and the workload question the Herald carried yesterday morning answered itself by the third inning.7 Tampa Bay's leather answered Cleveland's besides: Williamson dove to rob Ramírez in the fourth, and Walls — "one of the best shortstops on the planet," per the opposing manager — spun in the grass behind second to end the fifth.5

So the scholars' arithmetic this paper offered Cleveland as comfort only yesterday changes its allegiance: in series knotted at two games apiece, the fifth game's winner has taken the argument in 46 cases of 69, and road winners of such fifth games in 21 of 28.3 Tampa Bay flies home wanting one victory for the third World's Series in franchise history, the visits of 2008 and 2020 having both ended in defeat — and should the Rays take it, the 122nd Series is guaranteed a first-time champion, for neither they nor the waiting Brewers have ever won one. Cleveland, whose 77 seasons without a title since 1948 stand as the game's longest sorrow, must now win twice in two nights on foreign carpet; "We need to rebound tomorrow," said Vogt, master of the available options.3 The 36,303 by the lake filed out quietly after 2 hours and 50 minutes of clear, 63-degree October. The dome tonight will be louder — the particulars of the sixth game are set out at the Elimination Desk below.

News Around the League

THE ELIMINATION DESK: PERALTA, SIX VICTORIES WITHOUT A DEFEAT AND AN 0.79 FIGURE SINCE THE SIX-AND-TWENTIETH OF AUGUST, TAKES THE BALL UNDER THE DOME TONIGHT — CLEVELAND ANSWERS BY COMMITTEE WITH WILLIAMS HELD FOR A SEVENTH GAME IT MUST FIRST EARN, AND THE TROP AWAITS THE FIRST PENNANT EVER CLINCHED ON ITS CARPET

The sixth game goes tonight at 8:08 at Tropicana Field, and the pitching ledgers could scarcely sit further apart. Tampa Bay hands the ball to Freddy Peralta — 10-11 with a 4.42 for the whole of his itinerant season, but 6-0 with a 0.79 earned-run average over nine appearances since August 26, including a 0.99 figure with 26 strikeouts across five starts under this very dome — fresh from six shutout innings in the second game and the two borrowed relief outs in the fourth that this paper recorded in its Sunday number.8 Cleveland must stitch its evening from the committee: Slade Cecconi may open, with Tanner Bibee — one-third of an inning pitched all month — and Joey Cantillo expected to carry roughly two innings apiece, the high-leverage men behind them. Gavin Williams, the round's great strikeout engine, is barred on short rest — "No, that's not an option," said Stephen Vogt, whose ace's fastball sagged from 99.2 to 95.4 miles the hour across five innings of the third game — and Foster Griffin and Parker Messick are both spent, so Williams waits instead upon a Tuesday seventh game his club must first earn.78 The committee's spokesman kept it short: "It's crunch time," said Cecconi. "Whatever they need, I'm ready for."7

The stage carries its own story. Tropicana Field, shuttered by Hurricane Milton two Octobers ago while the club kept house elsewhere, returned this season to harbor a 55-26 home campaign — the best in the game, jointly with Milwaukee's — and has yielded three victories in four postseason sittings; no Tampa Bay pennant has ever been clinched upon its carpet, the 2020 flag having been won as the home club of a neutral yard.10 Cleveland, for its part, has been in this hole before and climbed out — down two games to none against the White Sox only a round ago — and its manager declines all despair: "This is when this team thrives," says Vogt, and "if there's a group I'm betting on to get this done, it's our guys."78

THE PROCLAMATION DESK: 'WE'RE GOING TO WIN TOMORROW' — DÍAZ, FIVE HITS IN TWO NIGHTS AND THE LAST MAN STANDING FROM THE 2020 PENNANT-WINNERS, DECLARES THE ROUND CONCLUDED, WHILE THE CLEVELAND BATS HAVE MANAGED FOUR RUNS SINCE HALPIN'S WALLOP

Guarantees are rare currency in October, where the game collects its debts promptly, but Yandy Díaz issued one Sunday night with the serenity of a man reading from a bank book. "It's a great opportunity. All of us are thinking of it," the 35-year-old said of the pennant through the club's interpreter — "But it all ends tomorrow. We're going to win tomorrow."9 The affidavit behind the boast is in order: three hits Sunday atop two Saturday, safe arrival in seven of his eight October contests, and a leadoff post from which, in his manager Kevin Cash's four words, "He goes, we go." The longer ledger is in order too — the only man on the active roster remaining from the 2020 pennant-winners has now played 33 postseason games in a Tampa Bay uniform, more than any man in franchise history, and his 25 postseason hits trail only Randy Arozarena's 38 and B.J. Upton's 27 on the club's all-time roll, all atop a season of .293, 22 home runs and 85 driven in across a career-high 154 games.9

The men he proposes to dismiss are, at present, struggling to furnish a rebuttal. Since Petey Halpin's bat-flipping blow turned the third game — the high-water mark of Cleveland's October, as readers of this paper's Friday number will recall — the Cleveland bats have produced four runs in two games, yesterday's lone tally arriving on a groundout; the club neither leaves the yard nor manufactures by other means, and the round has tilted accordingly.10 Their manager's answer to the guarantee was not a counter-boast but a position report: "We don't have another choice."9

THE PROPRIETOR'S DESK: 'YOU WON'T BE SO CHEERY WHEN YOU LOSE FOR ANOTHER TWO-AND-TWENTY YEARS,' A RETIRED SCRIBE TOLD ATTANASIO AT HIS FIRST MILWAUKEE INTERVIEW IN 2004 — TWO-AND-TWENTY YEARS LATER, TO THE AUTUMN, THE MAN HOLDS A PENNANT

When Mark Attanasio was introduced as the Brewers' new owner on October 4, 2004, a long-retired reporter in the front row of his first media scrum offered a prophecy: "You won't be so cheery when you lose for another 22 years!" Twenty-two years had then passed since Milwaukee's only World's Series appearance, in 1982. Twenty-two years later, to the very autumn, Attanasio stood on the Dodger Stadium grass while his club celebrated a pennant, and permitted himself the obvious arithmetic: "Here we are, 22 years later."11

The intervening ledger rewards inspection. The front office he purchased counted about 130 full-time souls; it now counts more than 400. His first club played to .500 — Milwaukee's first non-losing season in 13 years — a 26-year postseason famine ended in 2008, and the last nine seasons have brought eight Octobers, six division flags and three pennant rounds, culminating in this year's franchise-record 103 victories and an 18-6 September.11 The owner confesses the summit frightened him more than the climb: "I was more nervous than I have ever been because this could actually happen," he said of the fourth game. "It's the first time I felt pressure — real pressure. And fortunately, our guys delivered." His president of business operations, the Milwaukee-born Rick Schlesinger, supplied the creed of the regime — ownership as "a public trust," the club "really, effectively, owned by the fans" and Attanasio its steward — and the Herald, which keeps a skeptical eye on the proprietor class as a body, notes without irony that this is precisely the manner of stewardship it recommends to the other 29.11

THE APPRENTICE DESK: 'WE HIT UNTIL OUR HANDS WERE BLEEDING' — PRATT, A SHORTSTOP OF TWO-AND-TWENTY RAISED ON NIGHTLY BATTING IN A MISSISSIPPI YARD, CARRIES A .310 OCTOBER INTO THE WORLD'S SERIES

The pennant-winners' shortstop is a rookie who turned 22 during his first big-league season and plays the position as though he has held it for a decade. Cooper Pratt batted .281 with a .350 on-base mark across 74 games after his summons to Milwaukee, and has raised the figure to .310 through the club's October — an apprenticeship conducted in the loudest classrooms the game offers.12

The making of him was nightly and unglamorous. His father Russell, a college player at Utah who runs a youth baseball concern in northern Mississippi, had Cooper and his elder brother Ozzie — later of Ole Miss — hitting nearly every evening, no days off granted or requested. "We hit until our hands were bleeding," the young man reports, adding with candor, "I hated it for the longest time." His mother Heidi played college softball before becoming a family physician; the household's verdict on his temperament is unanimous. "He's so level, so steady. Never too up, never too down," says the father. Milwaukee took him in the sixth round of the 2023 draft and paid above the slot to sign him, and its infield coach Matt Erickson now suspects "a really high ceiling as a defender that maybe he didn't even know about." The apprentice's own summation wants no ornament: "This has always been my dream."12

The forward ledger is one line with a continent of weight in it: the sixth game of the American round tonight at 8:08 under the dome at St. Petersburg, a seventh there Tuesday only if Cleveland insists, and the World's Series opening Friday, the 23rd, at Milwaukee against whichever club survives.2 One side has promised the matter concluded; the other climbed out of this same hole only a round ago. The Herald ventures no guarantee of its own save the standing one — that tomorrow's number will carry the full account, pennant or stay of execution. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: TWO HUNDRED SIXTY-FOUR SUCH BLOWS HAD ALWAYS LEFT THE YARD, AND THE TWO HUNDRED SIXTY-FIFTH DIED IN HALPIN'S GLOVE — YET CAMINERO AND HIS FELLOWS WOULD NOT BE REFUSED, AND THE AMERICAN QUESTION STANDS LEVEL AT TWO GAMES APIECE: RAYS 7, GUARDIANS 3
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 102 · Sunday, the Eighteenth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 1 contest from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

TWO HUNDRED SIXTY-FOUR SUCH BLOWS HAD ALWAYS LEFT THE YARD, AND THE TWO HUNDRED SIXTY-FIFTH DIED IN HALPIN'S GLOVE — YET CAMINERO AND HIS FELLOWS WOULD NOT BE REFUSED, AND THE AMERICAN QUESTION STANDS LEVEL AT TWO GAMES APIECE: RAYS 7, GUARDIANS 3

Petey Halpin crashes into the center-field wall to rob Junior Caminero of a drive that, by the ledger of every like ball struck since the measuring instruments went up, had never once stayed in a ballpark — and Caminero answers two innings later with the go-ahead double anyway; Jonathan Aranda, hitless in ten tries entering the night, collects three hits and two runs batted in; Yandy Díaz closes the account with a two-run homer to the opposite field in the ninth; and Nick Martinez's 5 1/3 innings of one-run ball, preserved by two borrowed outs from Freddy Peralta, square the pennant round and guarantee its return to St. Petersburg on Monday

Begin with the cruelest out of the month. In the fourth inning Saturday night at Progressive Field, Junior Caminero struck a ball 110.7 miles the hour at the sweet-spot angle — and since the league's measuring instruments began their ledger in 2015, 264 balls had been hit so, and all 264 were home runs. The 265th hung in the frigid lakefront air nearly six full seconds while Petey Halpin ran a crooked, backpedaling errand to the deepest corner of center field, gathered it at the base of the wall, and struck the barrier with a thud the yard heard twice over. "For that to stay in the yard, it's got to do some funky stuff," said the robbed man's robber; "100%," said Caminero, asked if he thought it gone.7 Foster Griffin, who threw the pitch, called the play unbelievable and the ball a home run in any number of other parks.7

Cleveland's luck, having spent itself so extravagantly on one catch, ran dry thereafter. Caminero returned in the sixth and laced Daniel Espino's offering 110.2 miles the hour over the leaping José Ramírez into the left-field corner, cashing Jonathan Aranda for the lead, then stood atop second base in his October layers beating his chest at his own dugout.34 It was the awakening the Rays had waited a round for. Their celebrated top three — Díaz, Aranda and Caminero, whom the manager Kevin Cash needles in lean weeks as los tres pequeños, the three little ones — had come to Cleveland a combined 5-for-34 with one run batted in and 13 strikeouts; on Saturday they went 6-for-14 and drove in five. Aranda, hitless in the series at nightfall, finished 3-for-4; Díaz doubled, then sealed the business in the ninth with a two-run homer carried just over the right-field wall, opposite-field work of the barrel-chested old school.43 "It was just a matter of time for us three to get going," said Aranda through the club's interpreter.4

The pitching held up its end with room to spare. Nick Martinez, 36 years of age and master of three fastballs and a changeup he refused to abandon after spiking it early, allowed Steven Kwan's first-inning single and Chase DeLauter's run-scoring knock — DeLauter promptly cut down stretching for two by Victor Mesa Jr.'s sliding stop and throw — and then retired 11 men in succession, handing over 5 1/3 innings of one-run ball and collecting the first postseason victory of his long career. "He did a lot of Nick things out there," certified Cash.5 When Martinez departed with a man aboard in the sixth, the relief was Freddy Peralta — the Game 2 starter, lately of the Mets, whose between-starts throw-day the Rays simply relocated from the bullpen mound to the sixth inning of a pennant round. He recorded his two outs and kept the lead at one. "I'm just a reliever," he teased the writers afterward. "Why do you want to talk to me?" His starter answered for them: "He saved our game today."6

The seventh settled it, and unkindly for the home nine. Richie Palacios and Taylor Walls scored on Aranda's single to right, which skipped under DeLauter's glove for two bases more and an unearned third run when Chandler Simpson's sacrifice fly followed. "Put that one on me," said DeLauter, declining every excuse offered him. "You miss a ground ball and give up two runs — essentially give up three."11 Cleveland answered gamely — Travis Bazzana's first postseason homer and Brayan Rocchio's run-scoring single made it 5-3, and Kwan finished the evening with gauze packed in a lip he split diving into first base — but no nearer.8 So the round stands two games apiece, a best-of-three with the home dome recovered: the fifth game goes this very evening at five o'clock by the lake, Drew Rasmussen against the rookie Parker Messick, and the sixth is now guaranteed for Monday night at St. Petersburg.32 The scholars' comfort for Cleveland, who stood one swing from a three-games-to-one grip: in series knotted at two, the fifth game's winner has taken the argument in 46 cases of 69.8 The 33,355 who sat through 46 degrees of partly cloudy went home with the same arithmetic.1

News Around the League

THE PIVOT DESK: THE FIFTH GAME GOES AT FIVE O'CLOCK THIS EVENING, AND THE RAINOUT'S STRANGE GIFTS ARE NOW PLAIN — RASMUSSEN ON HIS ACCUSTOMED FIFTH DAY AGAINST MESSICK MOVED UP A GAME, WITH A PENNANT'S WORTH OF LEVERAGE ON THE TABLE

Friday's washout, which this paper mourned at the time, has proved an even-handed quartermaster. Drew Rasmussen takes the ball for Tampa Bay tonight on the five days' rest he kept nearly all season — his October account stands at 14 innings, two runs, two walks and 17 strikeouts across two starts, atop a 16-5, 2.67 regular campaign — while Cleveland, as this paper supposed yesterday it might, moves Parker Messick up from his appointed sixth game to the fifth, on normal rest, precisely because the postponement shoved the calendar a day.1081 The rookie left-hander's season now runs to 198 innings, the sixth-most by a first-year man in the last 20 years and far past his previous high of 138 1/3; his manager has allowed that some October command trouble may be the workload talking. The rookie himself files no grievance: "Honestly, my body feels great. To be able to take the ball in this game shows the confidence the team has in me."98

The stakes require no embroidery: the winner flies to St. Petersburg tonight holding three games of the four won and one victory from the World's Series; the loser bats for his life Monday. Cleveland's manager Stephen Vogt declares himself unshaken — "I'll put our guys up against any team in the world in a three-game series" — and holds in reserve a rested late guard of Hunter Gaddis, Erik Sabrowski and Cade Smith, none of whom worked in Saturday's seven-man bullpen procession.108 Tampa Bay, for its part, wanted exactly this: "That was one of the main objectives that we had here coming into Cleveland, just to force the series back home," said Jonathan Aranda. The forecast, for once, has nothing to say: clear and cold by the lake.10

THE WAITING DESK: SEVEN FULL DAYS OF IDLENESS FOR THE PENNANT-HOLDERS, THE LONGEST SIT OF ANY FLAG-WINNER SAVE THE '07 ROCKIES — AND THE LEDGER ON LONG RESTS READS EXACTLY EVEN, THOUGH THE RECENT PAGES LEAN AGAINST THE RESTED

Milwaukee's reward for sweeping its round by Thursday is a week of waiting: seven full days between the pennant and Friday's first game of the World's Series, the club's longest pause since spring training and the second-longest any flag-winner has endured since the championship rounds went to seven games in 1985. Only the 2007 Rockies sat longer — eight days, after winning 21 of 22 — and they were promptly swept by Boston, a precedent Milwaukee is free to decline.12

The full accounting is studiedly neutral. Since the postseason took its three-round shape in 1995, clubs entering the Series with the extra rest stand exactly 15-15; clubs that sat five full days or more, as the Brewers will, went 10-10. But the recent pages lean the other way — since 2009 the club that clinched its pennant first has gone 4-12 in the Series, and from 2009 through 2017 the less-rested club won nine straight.12 The sweep itself cuts both ways: of the 11 previous clubs that reached the Series by sweeping a seven-game round, only four finished the job — though the three most recent of them, the 2019 Nationals, 2022 Astros and 2025 Dodgers, all did.12 The Suds men may prefer the simplest reading: the first game goes Friday evening at their own yard, and nobody idle has lost anything yet.122

THE SHORTSTOP DESK: DOMBROWSKI SERVES NOTICE ON HIS $300 MILLION MAN — MEND THE GLOVE BY SPRING OR QUIT THE POSITION, PHILADELPHIA TELLS TURNER, AFTER A SEASON OF ONE-AND-TWENTY ERRORS

The bluntest sentence of the young offseason was pronounced in Philadelphia. Dave Dombrowski, the Quakers' president of baseball operations, summoned Trea Turner to Citizens Bank Park on Tuesday and told the shortstop — seven years and $190 million still owed on his $300 million engagement — that his defense must recover or his position will. "He knows he has to be better at shortstop," Dombrowski reported. "I told him it's really mandatory that it's like that. You cannot play shortstop like you did defensively in '26 going to '27."13

The indictment is in the ledger: Turner, 33, batted .242 with a .675 on-base-plus-slugging — perhaps the worst season of his career — and committed 21 errors at shortstop, the most in the league, before going 1-for-11 in the Wild Card defeat at Atlanta's hands. The remedies sketched are several: Turner to the outfield, which he does not prefer; Bryson Stott across the bag to shortstop; the prospect Aidan Miller, recovered from a year lost to his back, competing for a place by spring. Turner, to his credit, filed no appeal — "I've got a lot of work to do," he said. "Find answers. See what I did bad."13 The man's no-trade clause makes him all but immovable, so the parties are wedded to the repair — and with a work stoppage reckoned all but certain come December, the winter may afford him more drilling time than anyone would wish.13 The Herald, whose sympathies in such matters are on record, merely notes that a club which can owe one workman $190 million has settled the question of whether the till is empty.

THE AUCTION DESK: THE WINTER MARKET'S CROWN LOT IS ALREADY POSTED — SKUBAL, RENTED BY LOS ANGELES AT THE COST OF TWO PROSPECTS OF THE FIRST RANK, NOW STANDS TO COMMAND THE RICHEST PITCHING CONTRACT EVER LET

The Dodgers' early exit opens the bidding season, and the first lot is the grandest. Tarik Skubal heads a class of nine Los Angeles free agents — Kiké Hernández, Evan Phillips, Alex Vesia, Blake Treinen and the retiring Miguel Rojas among the others — and is reckoned the top player on the whole market. Los Angeles paid dearly for its three months of him at the summer deadline: the ready-made starter River Ryan, the outfield prospect Zyhir Hope and the right-hander Brady Smith, all to Detroit, for a rental now concluded.14

The walk-year ledger holds up its end. Skubal went 12-7 with a 2.72 earned-run average across 26 starts split between the Tigers and Dodgers, despite six weeks lost to a left elbow operation; last winter he took a record $32 million from Detroit in the arbitration room — an award this desk files among the honest victories of the workingman's side of the ledger — and he is now widely expected to surpass Yoshinobu Yamamoto's twelve-year, $325 million engagement as the largest guarantee ever extended a pitcher.14 Whether Los Angeles, which must also weigh the futures of its own young men, re-enters the bidding for the man it rented is the question Chavez Ravine will chew on all winter; the pitcher himself, asked after Thursday's elimination, preferred not to discuss it.14

The forward ledger is brief and loud: the fifth game of the American round this evening at five o'clock by the lake, the sixth Monday night at St. Petersburg, and a seventh Tuesday at the same address only if the argument insists; the World's Series opens Friday, the 23rd, at Milwaukee, where the hosts wait out the week in enforced leisure.2 By tomorrow's number one club will stand a single victory from the pennant, and the other will be rehearsing arguments for a Monday jury. The Herald will be at its post for all of it. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: Postseason Off-Day Edition — the Seventeenth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 101 · Saturday, the Seventeenth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the pennant races rest.

0 days until the fourth game of the American League's pennant round — the Rays at the Guardians, eight o'clock this very evening by the lake (Saturday, the 17th of October, 2026).

News Around the League

THE TARPAULIN DESK: THE SKY HOLDS ITS VETO OVER THE LAKE AND THE FOURTH GAME NEVER THROWS A PITCH — THE AMERICAN ROUND MOVES WHOLESALE TO TONIGHT AT EIGHT, SUNDAY SURRENDERS ITS DAY OF REST, AND THE DOME STANDS BY FOR MONDAY

The washout this paper feared only yesterday arrived on schedule and stayed past all bargaining. Rain settled over Progressive Field through Friday afternoon and declined every invitation to leave; the grounds crew swept standing water from the infield tarpaulin and chased the pools collecting on the warning track; a party of Tampa Bay pitchers emerged to play catch near the appointed hour and promptly thought better of it; and late in the evening the league called the thing off. "It never cleared out the way they were hoping it would," said Kevin Cash, who allowed that the league and both clubs "did everything they could to try to get it in." His opposite number took the longer view of local meteorology. "This is baseball. This is Cleveland," said Stephen Vogt. "We're more than used to these kinds of days."3

The week is accordingly redrawn, precisely as this paper warned it might be. The fourth game goes tonight at eight o'clock by the lake; the fifth follows Sunday at five o'clock, the scheduled day of rest stricken from the calendar; and should the argument require a sixth and a seventh, they wait at the Gulf Coast dome Monday and Tuesday nights.36 The standing of the quarrel is untouched by weather: the Lake Erie men lead it two games to one and may yet take the pennant without packing a trunk, while the Tampa men must win three of the four that remain. Even the ticket desk is shuffled with the games — Friday's stubs are good for Sunday, and Saturday's stand exactly where they are. The forecast, for its part, has repented: nothing heavier than ordinary October is projected tonight, the thermometer bound for 40 degrees by the late innings.3

THE CHESSBOARD DESK: A FREE DAY TO RESHUFFLE AND NEITHER MANAGER TOUCHES A PIECE — MARTINEZ KEEPS THE BALL FOR TAMPA BAY, ARMSTRONG STILL OPENS FOR CLEVELAND, AND THE TRUE MANEUVERING IS SAVED FOR SUNDAY

A postponement hands each side the rarest October commodity — choice — and both clubs promptly declined it. Nick Martinez, 15-6 with a 3.10 mark on the year, takes the ball tonight for the Gulf Coast club exactly as he would have Friday, and Cash would commit to nothing beyond him: "We'll go day to day from there." The logic wants little defending. Martinez has thrown 13 scoreless innings against these same Guardians over two regular-season meetings; his 2.38 figure on the road stood fourth in the American League — behind a list that includes, pointedly, Cleveland's own Parker Messick — and the Rays have gone 23-9 when he starts. "Nick's been a leader for us all year. He's been the bridge that's held us together," says Chandler Simpson. "When he's on the mound, we know our leader's on the mound."4

The deferred riches come later. Drew Rasmussen — worked hard of late, with a career-high 114 pitches in his final regular-season turn and better than 90 in each of two October starts since — now lines up for Sunday's fifth game on the five days' rest he kept nearly all season, and Freddy Peralta, warm off his Game 2 gem, stands ready for a sixth game should the series reach the dome.4 Cleveland's answer is the bullpen day it had long pencilled in for this spot: Shawn Armstrong, 2-1 with a 4.58 mark, opens — "Armstrong's going to start for us tomorrow," said Vogt on Friday night, and then said it again, in the manner of a man closing a subject — with Foster Griffin rested and unnamed but conspicuously available for the bulk innings behind him, and Tanner Bibee, Joey Cantillo and Slade Cecconi all in reserve. The rookie Messick, who started the second game, could move up to Sunday, when a pennant may sit on the table.5 And the idle Friday fattened both bullpens — no small mercy for the Lake Erie men, who have ridden Cade Smith and Hunter Gaddis hard through the month.3

THE HOMEFRONT DESK: THE CREAM CITY REARRANGES ITSELF AROUND FRIDAY — THE BASKETBALL CLUB MOVES ITS OPENING NIGHT TO MID-AFTERNOON FOR GAME ONE OF THE 122ND WORLD'S SERIES, AND THE FOOTBALL COACH TURNS UP IN A BREWERS CAP

Milwaukee's first World's Series since 1982 opens Friday next, the 23rd of October, at American Family Field — the first game of the 122nd Fall Classic, the National League's champion hosting whichever club survives the week by the lake — and the city has begun clearing its calendar accordingly.62 The Bucks, the town's basketball concern, were booked to raise the curtain on their own season at the Fiserv Forum that very evening; the club and its league have moved the tip-off from seven o'clock to three, "in recognition of this historic occasion," so that no Milwaukeean need choose between openings.7

"The Brewers' return to the World Series for the first time in 44 years is a special moment for Milwaukee and sports fans across Wisconsin," the basketball men declared, promising to cheer the baseball club from down the street. And up the road in Green Bay, Matt LaFleur, who coaches the football eleven, took Friday's press conference in a Brewers cap. "I want to support the Brewers," he said. "That was pretty cool to watch last night."7 The Suds men themselves, swept to the pennant and idle until their opponent is named, can only watch the lake with the rest of us.

THE TWO-WAY DESK: 'YES, DEFINITELY' — OHTANI, SILENT ON THE MOUND SINCE THE THIRD OF JULY, VOWS TO PITCH IN 2027, THOUGH WHETHER THE WINTER INCLUDES THE SURGEONS IS A QUESTION HE LEAVES OPEN

Shohei Ohtani's season ended Thursday night in the on-deck circle, bat in hand, and his first public business of the offseason was to promise both halves of himself back. Asked after the Angelenos' season-closing 6-4 defeat whether he means to pitch next year, the four-time Most Valuable answered through his interpreter without a comma's hesitation: "Yes, definitely. And looking forward to having a better season next year." Whether the road back runs through an operating theater is not yet settled — "hard to tell at this point," he allowed; it is "something that's going to be analyzed, discussed over the offseason."8

The mound half of him was, while it lasted, superb: a 1.79 earned-run average and a .179 mark against across 85 2/3 innings. But the left knee began complaining on June 11, the final four starts leaked 12 earned runs in 24 2/3 innings where all the work before had allowed 5 in 61, and after the third of July he did not pitch again — a September fortnight on the injured list for the right biceps, his first such visit in nearly three years, closing the ledger. This paper carried his insistence Wednesday that he could help with the bat regardless, and he did, the three-run homer in Thursday's finale ending a drought of two months. The career figures explain the stubbornness: among starters with 500 innings pitched since 1969, only Jim Palmer, Jacob deGrom and Clayton Kershaw own a better earned-run average than his 2.83.8

THE LEATHER DESK: THE SHAKIEST GLOVE OF 2025 IS A FINALIST FOR THE GOLD OF 2026 — SIMPSON LEARNS OF HIS NOMINATION FROM HIS OWN TELEPHONE IN A CLEVELAND HOTEL, AND THE COACH WHO REBUILT HIM SHARES THE CREDIT

The Rawlings nominations this paper recorded Thursday carried one story worth telling on its own. Chandler Simpson, the Rays' left fielder, woke in his Cleveland hotel Wednesday, took up his telephone for the morning's idle scrolling, and found himself tagged in congratulations: a Gold Glove finalist, alongside Cody Bellinger of the Yankees and Wyatt Langford of the Rangers, the verdicts sealed until the first of November. "Oh, wow," the 25-year-old reports thinking. "OK, cool."9

The arithmetic of the conversion is the story. A year ago the league's accounting had Simpson at minus-5 outs above average, the 11th percentile of all defenders; this season he stands at plus-8, the 93rd, and the runs-saved ledger swung from minus-9 to plus-8. The credit is shared, by every account including the manager's, with Corey Dickerson, the first-base coach and former outfielder whose daily instruction taught the fastest man in the league to read the ball off the bat and stand where it was going. "I think that is maybe one of the coolest stories of our season, where he was defensively last year, where he's come to this year," said Cash.9 Nor is the glove the whole of the tale: when Friday's rained-out lineup was posted, Simpson stood third in the batting order — contact and speed deployed where sluggers ordinarily reside — and the assignment is expected to survive to tonight.3

October has now emptied three Fridays running — twice by the bracket's own design, and last night by the sky's veto. What remains is simply told: the American question resumes tonight at eight by the lake, continues Sunday at five with no day of rest between, and removes to the Gulf Coast dome Monday and Tuesday only if Tampa Bay makes it necessary; Milwaukee waits on the far side with Friday's curtain already hung.36 A pennant may be had by Sunday evening, or the argument may run the whole week — either way the Herald will be at its post with the full account. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
