entry.title: THE LAST BALL OF THE NATIONAL LEAGUE'S YEAR COMES DOWN IN CHOURIO'S GLOVE — DOWN FOUR RUNS BEFORE THE SECOND INNING HAD COOLED, THE BREWERS CLIMB OUT A SIXTH TIME THIS OCTOBER, SWEEP THE TWICE-CROWNED CHAMPIONS FROM THEIR OWN YARD, AND CARRY MILWAUKEE TO ITS FIRST WORLD'S SERIES SINCE 1982: BREWERS 6, DODGERS 4
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 100 · Friday, the Sixteenth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 2 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE LAST BALL OF THE NATIONAL LEAGUE'S YEAR COMES DOWN IN CHOURIO'S GLOVE — DOWN FOUR RUNS BEFORE THE SECOND INNING HAD COOLED, THE BREWERS CLIMB OUT A SIXTH TIME THIS OCTOBER, SWEEP THE TWICE-CROWNED CHAMPIONS FROM THEIR OWN YARD, AND CARRY MILWAUKEE TO ITS FIRST WORLD'S SERIES SINCE 1982: BREWERS 6, DODGERS 4

Shohei Ohtani's three-run homer — his first in two months, ending the longest drought of his career — stakes Los Angeles to a 4-0 lead in the second inning, and Milwaukee answers the way it has answered all month: back-to-back doubles from William Contreras and Jake Bauers, a bases-loaded walk, Garrett Mitchell's go-ahead drive in the sixth and David Hamilton's parting shot in the ninth, while Aaron Ashby records the final nine outs; no club had ever erased a four-run deficit to finish a postseason sweep, and no club had ever been swept by an opponent one October and swept that same opponent the next

The National League's season ended in the glove of Jackson Chourio, on a fly ball that died just short of the left-center warning track at Dodger Stadium on Thursday night, and the noise that followed belonged to the visitors' dugout and to the several thousand Wisconsinites among the 49,104 who declined to go home. They stayed to watch the Warren C. Giles Trophy presented on enemy ground, and they were entitled: Milwaukee has waited 44 years for this, since the 1982 club of Harvey's Wallbangers carried the American League's flag and lost a seven-game World's Series to St. Louis. This pennant is the franchise's first in the National League — and the cry of that earlier October, "Milwaukee, you have a World Series!", belonged by the record not to Bob Uecker but to his partner Dwayne Mosley, Uecker having slipped down to the clubhouse to ready the celebration broadcast. The city may now compose a new one.43

The evening began as the champions' best of the month. Shane Drohan opened for Milwaukee and walked two; Dustin May inherited the second inning and absorbed four runs of it — Andy Pages' single for the first, and then Shohei Ohtani, restored to the leadoff post he had not occupied since September 27, turning a 1-1 cutter into a three-run drive to right-center. It was Ohtani's first home run since August 18, the end of a 115-plate-appearance drought, the longest of his career, whose every barren week this paper has chronicled.38 From 4-0 the ledger turned by installments. Contreras and Bauers struck back-to-back doubles in the fourth, Bauers' a ground-rule bounce worth two runs; in the fifth David Hamilton singled home Sal Frelick and Bauers drew a bases-loaded walk for the tie; in the sixth Garrett Mitchell led off against the left-hander Tanner Scott and hit the go-ahead homer to center; and in the ninth Hamilton — the nine-hole man, two hits, two runs driven in and a stolen base on his evening — added a parting shot off Edwin Díaz's hanging slider.3

The final nine outs belonged to Aaron Ashby, on 39 pitches, and they were not uneventful: he stranded the tying run in scoring position in both the seventh and the eighth, striking out Ohtani swinging with that run at third base. The save ran three full innings in a pennant-clincher, company he shares with only Lance McCullers Jr., Madison Bumgarner, Steve Howe and Vida Blue since the save became an official statistic in 1969; his October account now shows 12 1/3 innings and no runs across six errands.87 The relief corps as a body allowed five runs in 21 2/3 innings of the round, a 2.08 figure, and Joel Romero's victory Thursday meant a reliever won all four games of the series — a thing no best-of-seven sweep had ever shown — and seven of Milwaukee's eight games this postseason, which no club had done either.75

Mitchell's blow deserves its biography. Diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes at nine years old, he slid to the 20th selection of his draft on the doubts that diagnosis bred, wears an insulin pod wired to his telephone, and has played more games this season than in his first four years combined. On Wednesday he and Bauers struck back-to-back homers off a left-hander — lefty upon lefty, a sequence only Ruth and Gehrig in 1928 and Schwarber and Harper earlier this very month had written before them — and on Thursday he supplied the pennant's deciding run. "It was time to make the big shift," said his father Antony, who reports that his son has always run on doubt as other men run on praise.6

The ledger of the series reads like a page from the game's far shelf. The four-run recovery is the largest ever to finish a postseason sweep, and ties the largest in any pennant-clinching game since the rounds began in 1969, matching the Yankees of 2000 and 2003; Milwaukee trailed in all four games of a series it swept, which no club had done; its six comeback victories in its first eight October games stand alone in the records.5 The Brewers are the fifth club to sweep a reigning champion from a best-of-seven — after the 1990 Reds, 1966 Orioles, 1963 Dodgers and 1914 Braves, every one of whom went on to the World's Series — and the first ever, in this sport, to be swept by an opponent one postseason and sweep that same opponent whole the next, the wound of last year's four-game dismissal at these same hands repaid to the penny. This was the 11th best-of-seven ever played between two 100-win clubs and the first to end in a sweep, and Los Angeles even lost its first October game of the year with Tyler Glasnow pitching, a distinction the man had carried through seven appearances.53 The valedictories were brief. "We got outplayed in all facets," said Dave Roberts. "You remember it," said Pat Murphy of the beatings his club once took in this yard. "You have to have that faith," said the captain Christian Yelich, "and you have to have, like, the belief that you know this group can get it done."34 The World's Series opens Friday next, October 23, at American Family Field, against the winner of the American round — whose state of play the Postseason Card takes up below.142

The Postseason Card

THE EIGHTH MAN IN THE ORDER SENDS HIS BAT SKYWARD AND THE BALL TO THE BLEACHERS — HALPIN'S TWO-RUN WALLOP OVERTURNS AN AFTERNOON SIMPSON'S TRIPLE HAD BRIEFLY STOLEN, WILLIAMS FANS NINE MORE IN FIVE, AND THE CLEVELAND NINE STAND TWO WINS FROM THE WORLD'S SERIES: GUARDIANS 3, RAYS 2

October baseball by daylight, at the one-o'clock hour the rain dictated, and 30,101 fill the lakefront yard anyway; Gavin Williams strikes out nine of the eighteen men he faces and departs early by design, Chandler Simpson's two-strike triple gives Tampa Bay a short-lived lead, and Petey Halpin — a reserve outfielder a fortnight ago — answers with a two-run homer off Griffin Jax and a bat flip his own bullpen scored a ten, before Cade Smith's four-out save sends Cleveland ahead two games to one

The afternoon appointment this paper commended yesterday to readers of flexible luncheon arrangements proved worth the leave-taking. Under a sunny 62 degrees at Progressive Field — the one-o'clock start having been dictated by the evening's forecast — 30,101 turned out on a weekday midday and were repaid in two hours and twenty-eight minutes. Cleveland struck first in the second, Nathaniel Lowe lining a double to right to cash Jo Adell; Tampa Bay answered in the fourth when Chandler Simpson, down to his last strike, lashed a two-run triple past Chase DeLauter to score Yandy Díaz and Victor Mesa Jr. — the speedster's third run driven in of the round, and very nearly the whole of the visitors' offense.10

The reply came from the eighth place in the order. Patrick Bailey singled with one out in the fifth, and Petey Halpin — until a fortnight ago a late-innings defensive reserve, pressed into the lineup in the Chicago round and never since removed — turned Griffin Jax's 96-mile sinker into the right-field bleachers, 105 off the bat, for the lead. The bat went skyward in a high, turning arc. "I just kind of blacked out," Halpin pleaded afterward — October's fashionable alibi, Jake Bauers having entered the same one at the dome on Monday. "It was majestic," certified Steven Kwan; Daniel Espino, warming in the bullpen, scored the flip a ten while confessing he feared the lumber might strike its owner on the way down.11

Gavin Williams made the two runs stand. Five innings, two hits, nine strikeouts — both runs rode Simpson's triple — and a departure at 70 pitches that his manager called precaution rather than necessity. The figures behind the figures: 33 strikeouts in 16 2/3 innings this October, a 45.9 percent strikeout rate that is the highest any pitcher has carried through a postseason of ten innings or more, past Corey Knebel's 44.6; no Cleveland pitcher before him had struck out nine or better in three straight postseason starts; and his 45 October strikeouts for the franchise passed Andrew Miller for fourth on the all-time roll, behind Charles Nagy's 55, Orel Hershiser's 54 and Corey Kluber's 47.1012 Behind him Espino, Erik Sabrowski and Hunter Gaddis carried the ball to Cade Smith, whose four-out save ran his month to a 1.00 earned-run average with 13 strikeouts in nine innings. Tampa Bay's consolations were small but genuine: Liam Hicks threw out two Cleveland runners, the first Rays catcher ever to cut down two in a postseason game.12

The visitors' grief is the bats. Three hits and 13 strikeouts on the afternoon; Junior Caminero 0-for-4 with four of them, his first postseason homer still unstruck; the top third of the order — Díaz, Jonathan Aranda, Caminero — a combined 1-for-12. "We have to make adjustments and play our baseball," Caminero said through the club's interpreter, and his manager Kevin Cash asked plainly for bigger at-bats.10 So Cleveland leads two games to one and stands two victories from its first World's Series since 2016 — the fourth time the franchise has held such a lead in a pennant round, having cashed the one in 1997 and let go those of 1998 and 2007 — while Tampa Bay trails at this station for the first time in its history; the scholars note the winner of a third game from a 1-1 tie has taken the series in roughly seven cases of ten.1012 The fourth game is appointed for eight o'clock tonight by the lake, weather permitting, and the Weather Desk sets out the particulars — and the contingencies — elsewhere in this number.2

News Around the League

THE LAUREL DESK: THE MOST VALUABLE MAN OF THE NATIONAL ROUND NEARLY QUIT THE GAME TWO WINTERS PAST — BAUERS, SIX RUNS DRIVEN IN AND A HIT IN EVERY GAME, IS THE FIRST BREWER EVER TO CARRY OFF THE HONOR, AND EITHER AMERICAN FINALIST IS A FORMER EMPLOYER

The hardware followed the story. Jake Bauers, whose twelve-pitch walk turned the second game and whose eleven-pitch homer turned the third — both sieges set out at length in these columns — was named the most valuable player of the National League's round on the field Thursday night, the first man in Milwaukee's history to take the series laurel. The affidavit: a hit in all four games, a team-leading six runs driven in — tied for the most in any postseason series the franchise has played — and in the clincher a two-run double and the bases-loaded walk that drew the game level.9

The man receives the honor at 31, in his seventh season, two winters removed from nearly leaving the game altogether before his wife talked him back onto the field. The regular season that followed ran to 26 home runs and 86 runs batted in, and October has compounded it. "I just let it all come to me," Bauers said. "I didn't chase it." His teammates were less restrained — "No one deserves it more," said Sal Frelick — and his manager chose the house style: "Jake played with a broken toe, he's had shin splints all year, and he's soft," offered Pat Murphy, entirely in jest.9 The footnote the deadball desks will savor: Bauers broke into the league with Tampa Bay in 2018 and spent two seasons in Cleveland's employ, so whichever club emerges from the American round, the World's Series will send the series' most valuable man against a former employer.9

THE WEATHER DESK: THE AMERICAN ROUND'S FOURTH GAME GOES TONIGHT AT EIGHT BY THE LAKE, IF THE SKY ALLOWS — MARTINEZ, WHO BLANKED CLEVELAND TWICE THIS SUMMER ACROSS THIRTEEN INNINGS, MEETS A HOME STAFF ASSEMBLED BY COMMITTEE, AND A WASHOUT WOULD REDRAW THE WEEK

The American League's fourth sitting is appointed for eight o'clock Eastern tonight at Progressive Field, Cleveland leading two games to one — but the sky holds a vote. Rain is in the Friday forecast, the same forecast that moved yesterday's game up to one o'clock in the afternoon, and both commands spent Thursday drawing contingencies. Should the evening prove unplayable, the clubs could pass Friday idle and play the fourth and fifth games Saturday and Sunday by the lake, spending the scheduled travel day, with a sixth game to follow at the Gulf without pause.132

If the game is played tonight, Tampa Bay sends Nick Martinez, a right-hander of career-high employment this season — 31 starts, a 15-6 record and a 3.10 earned-run average — who holds a peculiar mastery of the home side: two starts against Cleveland this summer, thirteen innings, not one run, including seven blank frames in a 1-0 verdict in this very yard in April. Drew Rasmussen stands slated for the fifth game and Freddy Peralta for the sixth.1312 Cleveland's answer is a committee: a bullpen evening in which Joey Cantillo is expected to carry a large share, Tanner Bibee and Slade Cecconi the bulk innings, and Shawn Armstrong — unscored upon in four October appearances — or Daniel Espino may be first out of the gate. A postponement would change the committee's complexion entirely, handing Foster Griffin the ball Saturday on regular rest. "Our guys stay ready," said Stephen Vogt, declining to be alarmed on either count.1312

THE ALMANAC DESK: THE WORLD'S SERIES OPENS FRIDAY NEXT AT MILWAUKEE — HOME GROUND EARNED BY A HUNDRED AND THREE VICTORIES, THE FIRST TWO GAMES AND ANY SIXTH AND SEVENTH BY THE LAKESIDE BREWERY, AND THE AMERICAN CHAMPION TO BE KNOWN BY THEN

The almanac may now be printed in ink. The 122nd World's Series opens Friday, October 23, at American Family Field in Milwaukee, with the second game there Saturday the 24th; the third, fourth and fifth games go Monday the 26th through Wednesday the 28th at the American champion's grounds; and a sixth and seventh, should the argument require them, return to Milwaukee on Friday the 30th and Saturday the 31st.142

The home ground is held on merit, not on league custom: the Brewers' 103-59 was the best record in the majors, a franchise mark, and it outranks whatever the American round produces — Tampa Bay having won 98 and Cleveland fewer still. Every game goes out over the FOX wire. Start times await the league's pleasure, and the opponent awaits tonight's weather; both will be entered in this ledger the morning after they are known.14

THE FAREWELL DESK: ROJAS, AGED SEVEN-AND-THIRTY, TELLS HIS TEAMMATES 'THIS IS IT' — THIRTEEN SEASONS, TWO TITLES, A NO-HITTER PRESERVED WITH THE BACKHAND AND A SEVENTH-GAME HOMER IN THE NINTH, AND NOW A DESK IN THE DODGERS' SCHOOLHOUSE

The last game of the National League's season was also the last of a distinguished career. Miguel Rojas, 37 years old, told his Los Angeles teammates after Thursday's defeat that he had played his final game as an active man: "This is it, guys. This is it." The ledger he closes runs thirteen major-league seasons and 21 years in professional baseball — a 2014 debut with these same Dodgers, remembered for the backhand stop at third base that helped preserve Clayton Kershaw's June no-hitter; eight seasons as Miami's everyday shortstop and captain; and a return to Los Angeles in 2023 for four seasons, 446 games and a .260 average.15

The crowning entries came late, as they sometimes do for the glove men: World's Series titles in 2024 and 2025, and in the seventh game of last autumn's Series against Toronto, a game-tying home run in the ninth inning — a swing that will outlive every fielding chart ever drawn of him. He does not go far: Rojas moves into a player-development post with the organization, the exact title still being lettered. "He built a legacy that we'll be talking about for a long time," said Freddie Freeman; Mookie Betts called him simply "our leader." The Herald tips its cap to a workman of the old school and wishes him a long second career teaching the backhand.15

With this number the Herald's ledger turns one hundred — a hundred mornings of scores set down and deeds sung since this desk first took up its pen, and the chronicle is pleased to mark the occasion with a pennant in it. The forward ledger now reads: the American round's fourth game tonight at eight by the lake, weather permitting, a fifth Saturday at the same address, and a sixth Monday at the Gulf should the argument run on; the National League's business is concluded until Friday next, the 23rd, when the World's Series opens at Milwaukee.213 One league's season ended last night in a glove in left-center; the other's hangs tonight on a rain cloud over Lake Erie. The game, as ever, keeps its own calendar and lets the rest of us guess. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: THE FIRST PITCH OF THE EVENING LEAVES THE YARD AND THE ELEVENTH OF A SINGLE SIEGE DECIDES IT — CHOURIO AMBUSHES SNELL BEFORE THE FIFTY THOUSAND HAVE SETTLED, BAUERS OUTLASTS HIM FOR A GO-AHEAD CLOUT, MITCHELL FOLLOWS HIM OVER THE BARRIER, AND MILWAUKEE STANDS ONE VICTORY FROM ITS FIRST WORLD'S SERIES IN FOUR-AND-FORTY YEARS: BREWERS 6, DODGERS 2
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 99 · Thursday, the Fifteenth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 1 contest from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE FIRST PITCH OF THE EVENING LEAVES THE YARD AND THE ELEVENTH OF A SINGLE SIEGE DECIDES IT — CHOURIO AMBUSHES SNELL BEFORE THE FIFTY THOUSAND HAVE SETTLED, BAUERS OUTLASTS HIM FOR A GO-AHEAD CLOUT, MITCHELL FOLLOWS HIM OVER THE BARRIER, AND MILWAUKEE STANDS ONE VICTORY FROM ITS FIRST WORLD'S SERIES IN FOUR-AND-FORTY YEARS: BREWERS 6, DODGERS 2

Jackson Chourio strikes Blake Snell's very first offering into the right-center seats — one year to the day after he opened a postseason game the same way — and after Will Smith's bases-loaded double briefly restores the champions and their crowd, Jake Bauers fouls off everything Snell has left and turns the eleventh pitch of the battle into a two-run homer, Garrett Mitchell makes it back-to-back, and the Dodgers stand three games down in a hole only one club in history has ever climbed out of

Dodger Stadium got its voice back in the sixth inning Wednesday night, and kept it for less than an inning. Will Smith, mired all month, had just lined a bases-loaded double off the top of the left-center wall for the lead, and the 50,708 were making the old championship noise — two titles running will teach a crowd the words. Then Jake Bauers stepped in against Blake Snell in the seventh and declined, pitch after pitch after pitch, to be put away, and when the eleventh offering caught too much of the plate he deposited it in the right-field pavilion, 412 feet off, for two runs and the lead.34 The yard went so quiet that the visitors' dugout could be heard celebrating in the upper deck. Garrett Mitchell struck the next homer himself, back-to-back, and Milwaukee had turned a 2-1 deficit into a 6-2 verdict and a three-games-to-none grip on the National League's pennant round.3

The evening had announced its character on its very first pitch. Jackson Chourio, 22 years old, met Snell's opening fastball — 97.6 miles the hour, center-cut — and drove it the opposite way into the right-center seats before some of the principals had found their places; the Milwaukee owner was still scrambling to his seat, and Bauers was still pulling on his batting gloves.6 The records went scrambling with him: only six men have opened a postseason game with a first-pitch home run since such things were first counted in 1988, and Chourio has now done it twice — one year to the day since he did it in this same round against this same club — a distinction he shares with George Springer alone. The blow was his sixth postseason homer, the most any Brewer has ever accumulated, and Snell became the only pitcher twice victimized by the leadoff ambush.6 The young man played the rest of his evening in company: a praying mantis took up residence on his shoulder in the third, just as he settled under a Freddie Freeman fly ball half-lost in the low sun, and could not be persuaded off him. The catch was made, insect and all.7

Between the first blow and the last ran a proper pitchers' evening. Snell, who had not allowed a home run in ten starts this year, gathered himself after Chourio's clout and at one stretch retired fourteen men in succession, nine strikeouts among his evening's work.54 Robert Gasser — the man this paper introduced yesterday as the season's quietest success — answered with five scoreless innings of his own, three hits, on 72 pitches. The sixth undid the visitors' arithmetic for a moment: Abner Uribe arrived from the bullpen without his compass, walked three Dodgers, and Smith's double cashed two of them — the heaviest damage Milwaukee's relief corps has absorbed all month, with a blown save entered against Uribe's account. DL Hall walked in, stranded Shohei Ohtani ninety feet from home, and the damage stopped at two.35

Then came the seventh, and the at-bat that may yet stand as the series' epitaph. Andrew Vaughn's seven-pitch walk ended Snell's run of fourteen straight; Christian Yelich went in to run for him; and Bauers — who turned the second game Monday with a twelve-pitch walk against Yoshinobu Yamamoto — began fouling off everything with a star on it. A called strike, two balls, a foul tip; two-strike fouls off the slider and the curve; ball three; then fouls off the four-seamer, the changeup, the slider again. The eleventh pitch was a fastball meant for the edge that arrived at the middle, and Bauers did not miss it. He is the second man in postseason history with plate appearances of eleven pitches or more in consecutive games — the Cubs' Aramis Ramirez, in 2003, is the other — and his homer was just the sixth ever struck on the eleventh pitch or later of a postseason at-bat.4 The beaten pitcher, once his teammate in the Tampa Bay chain, paid him the evening's handsomest tribute: "I've seen all the ups and downs he's been through, and it's been a lot of downs. For him to go through this right now, he's earned it. Hat's off to him. What an at-bat. I threw everything I had."4 This is, after all, a man Milwaukee itself released two Novembers ago, a journeyman of five organizations who once mused about quitting the game for Costa Rica. "I was looking for a fastball, and I didn't want to miss it," Bauers said. "I said I'll adjust to anything else, but if you get a heater, don't miss it."4

Mitchell's four-bagger made the pair the third set of back-to-back postseason homers in Milwaukee's annals and chased Snell; a wild pitch cashed Brice Turang in the eighth and Joey Ortiz singled home Cooper Pratt in the ninth, and the accounting was complete. The visitors have now answered, immediately and in kind, every one of the four innings in which Los Angeles has scored in this series — their fifth comeback victory in seven October games, a figure matched this early only by the 1996 Yankees and 1980 Phillies, both of whom finished their autumns with parades.3 The arithmetic ahead is the kind this paper prints with a steady hand: of the 42 clubs ever down three games to none in a best-of-seven, 32 were swept, two forced a seventh game, and exactly one — the 2004 Red Sox, on whose roster stood a reserve outfielder named Dave Roberts — recovered the series. "It's certainly possible," says the same Roberts, now managing the club that must do it. "I've lived it."5 His batsmen, 3-for-32 with runners in scoring position this postseason outside Smith's double, are rather further from the precedent than he is. Kyle Tucker states the assignment plainly: "This team's won four games before. That's what we're going to have to do."3 The fourth game goes this very evening at eight o'clock Eastern at Dodger Stadium, and the Elimination Desk takes up its particulars elsewhere in this number.10

News Around the League

THE ELIMINATION DESK: TONIGHT AT EIGHT THE CHAMPIONS BAT FOR THEIR LIVES BEHIND GLASNOW, UNDEFEATED COMPANY IN THIS OCTOBER'S SEVEN ERRANDS — MILWAUKEE, ASKED FOR ITS STARTER, PROMISES ONLY THAT 'THERE WILL BE PITCHING'

The National League's fourth sitting goes tonight at eight o'clock Eastern at Dodger Stadium — moved up an hour from nine by the league's Wednesday decree — with the sweep standing one game off and the champions' three-peat standing on its last legal appeal.810

Los Angeles sends its best remaining argument. Los Angeles has yet to lose a postseason game in which Tyler Glasnow has pitched this month — seven appearances, a 1.73 earned-run average across 26 innings — and the man carries a 3.60 figure in three career elimination games, all served in Tampa Bay's employ. His last outing wobbled, five walks against Atlanta in the Division round, but surrendered a single run in 4 2/3 innings.10 Behind him the bullpen reports in nearly full strength, though the first two games' starters do not: Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto are held back for a fifth and sixth game that will exist only if tonight is won.510

Milwaukee, meanwhile, conducted the week's briefest press conference. "Pitching tomorrow?" a reporter asked Pat Murphy, hoping for a name. "Yeah," the manager replied, "there will be pitching."10 The candidates for what amounts to a bullpen evening are plentiful and rested: the left-handers Kyle Harrison and Shane Drohan and the right-hander Chad Patrick have yet to throw a pitch in seven postseason games, and Dustin May — a former Dodger with a 2020 ring from this very ballpark — threw an inning in the second game. The staff they would front carries a 1.74 earned-run average this postseason, the lowest of the twelve clubs that entered.10 The champions have twice lately climbed from the brink — down two games to one against San Diego in 2024, down three games to two in last year's World's Series — but they have never needed four victories in a row with winter at the door. "We've never been in this big of a hole," says Kiké Hernández, "but we've had our backs against the wall plenty of times before, and we've come out of it."5

THE LAKEFRONT DESK: RAIN MOVES THE AMERICAN QUESTION TO ONE O'CLOCK IN THE AFTERNOON — WILLIAMS, NOW OFFICIAL, TAKES THE BALL FOR THE FOREST CITY NINE AGAINST JAX, WHO MAKES THE FIRST OCTOBER START OF HIS LIFE IN A YARD HE KNOWS BY HEART

The American League's pennant round resumes today at Progressive Field at one o'clock in the afternoon, Eastern — the league having moved the game up five full hours from its evening appointment on account of rain forecast over Cleveland tonight. October baseball by daylight, by the lake, with the round tied at a game apiece: the deadball desks could ask no better page.89

The pitching is now official on both sides. Gavin Williams, whom this paper reckoned yesterday the likely man, was formally named Wednesday afternoon — on regular rest at last, after a Division round in which he made two starts and an emergency relief errand, recorded the final three outs of the fourth game, and came back on one day's rest to strike out twelve in the fifth, tying the franchise's postseason record. His October ledger stands at a 1.54 earned-run average with 24 strikeouts in 11 2/3 innings, and today's assignment lines him up, should the series run its full length, to start a seventh game Tuesday on regular rest.9 Opposite him, Griffin Jax makes the first postseason start of his career — a starter most of this season, lately a reliever by October necessity, with a 0.90 earned-run average over his last five appearances; since a rough return from elbow discomfort in early September, he has permitted two runs in 20 innings with 19 strikeouts across his last four regular-season starts and a Division-round relief errand. The venue holds no mysteries for him: most of his career was spent in Minnesota's employ, and his 13 relief appearances in this very yard produced a 2.19 earned-run average. The man is presumably also acquainted with the weather.9

The crowd that sang Cleveland back from two defeats down against Chicago now gets three straight home dates with the round level — and the statisticians' note from yesterday's number still stands: the winner of a third game in a series tied at one has gone on to take the series in roughly seven cases of ten. Patrick Bailey, swinging a hot October bat, catches his customary partner; Tampa Bay's lone question is whether Jonny DeLuca or Cedric Mullins patrols center.9

THE MANAGERIAL DESK: THE COURTSHIP THIS PAPER REPORTED YESTERDAY LOSES ITS CHAPERONE — HOUSTON LETS ESPADA'S PAPERS LAPSE A DAY AFTER LENDING HIM TO SEATTLE'S PARLOR, AND PHILADELPHIA, TWICE REFUSED BY CORA, GIVES MATTINGLY, AGED FIVE-AND-SIXTY, TWO YEARS ON MERIT

The managerial market produced two settlements Wednesday, and the first reads as a sequel to yesterday's number. Joe Espada, whose permission to interview for Seattle's vacancy this paper reported only yesterday, will not be back in Houston at all: the Astros announced they will not renew his contract when it expires at the month's end. The owner Jim Crane supplied the customary warm send-off — "We are thankful for Joe's hard work, his passion for the game, and for his commitment to the Houston Astros" — and the club parted besides with five of its coaches, leaving it in search of a manager and a general manager at once, Dana Brown having been dismissed in August.12 The record Espada carries to market: 256 wins against 229 across three seasons, division flags in 2024 and 2026 — the latter at 81-81, the first club in the game's history to reach the postseason without a winning record — and a two-game sweep at the White Sox's hands for an exit. The courtship across the division may now proceed without asking anyone's leave.12

In Philadelphia, meantime, the interim tag came off. Don Mattingly, 65 years old, signed a two-year engagement as the Phillies' manager, the position he has held in fact since Rob Thomson's dismissal 28 games into the season. His case argued itself: 79 wins against 55 thereafter, a Wild Card berth clinched with a victory in the season's final game, and an exit in the deciding third game of the Wild Card round against Atlanta. The appointment carries its footnotes — the man is the father of the club's general manager Preston Mattingly, and the executive Dave Dombrowski was twice rebuffed in his pursuit of Alex Cora before settling, both times, on the man already in the chair.13 The Herald observes that 23 consecutive seasons of managing and coaching, laid atop a playing career of the first order, make "settling" a curious word for it.

THE AWARDS DESK: RAWLINGS NAMES THREE MEN TO EVERY POST FOR THE GOLDEN GLOVES, VERDICTS SEALED UNTIL THE FIRST OF NOVEMBER — AND TWO OF THE NOMINATED WILL BE AT WORK THIS VERY AFTERNOON BY THE LAKE

The leather trade published its short lists Wednesday: the Gold Glove finalists for 2026, three men to a position in each league, the utility post included, with the winners to be announced on the first of November. The electorate, for the record, is the league's 30 managers and up to six coaches per club, barred from voting for their own men and counting for three-quarters of the verdict, the remaining quarter supplied by the Society for American Baseball Research's defensive index.11 The Blue Jays and Cubs lead the nominations with five men apiece; the Braves, Diamondbacks, Rangers and Royals count four each.11

Two of the nominated have more immediate engagements. Tanner Bibee, a finalist among American League pitchers, and Taylor Walls, a finalist at shortstop, are presently employed on opposite sides of the pennant round that resumes at one o'clock today at Progressive Field — Bibee for Cleveland, Walls for Tampa Bay — and may be excused for leaving the campaigning to their rivals.11 The Herald reports nominations as nominations, per its standing rule: the hardware changes hands when the ballots are counted, and not an edition sooner.

Today the calendar grants both arguments at once, and at civilized intervals: the American question at one o'clock in the afternoon by the lake, where the rain rewrote the timetable, and the National at eight in Los Angeles, where Milwaukee may finish what it started and the champions must win tonight and then three more times besides. Friday holds the American round's fourth game at Cleveland, and a fifth National sitting — should tonight's defendants earn it.2 An afternoon playoff game is the oldest luxury the sport affords: it was how all of October sounded before the lights went up, and a reader with a flexible luncheon arrangement is advised to take full advantage. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: THE SECRET IS ANNOUNCED OVER THE LOUD-SPEAKER AND KEPT ANYWAY — ONE-AND-SEVENTY FASTBALLS FROM 'FASTBALL FREDDY,' THE SWIFTEST OF HIS NINE-YEAR LIFE; A GROUND BALL FINDS THE ONE CRACK IN THE LEAGUE'S SUREST THIRD BASEMAN; AND THE THROWBACK-CLAD RAYS SQUARE THE PENNANT ROUND: RAYS 3, GUARDIANS 1
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 98 · Wednesday, the Fourteenth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 1 contest from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE SECRET IS ANNOUNCED OVER THE LOUD-SPEAKER AND KEPT ANYWAY — ONE-AND-SEVENTY FASTBALLS FROM 'FASTBALL FREDDY,' THE SWIFTEST OF HIS NINE-YEAR LIFE; A GROUND BALL FINDS THE ONE CRACK IN THE LEAGUE'S SUREST THIRD BASEMAN; AND THE THROWBACK-CLAD RAYS SQUARE THE PENNANT ROUND: RAYS 3, GUARDIANS 1

Kevin Cash grumbles that even the public-address man was advertising 'Fastball Freddy' before the first pitch — then Peralta throws 71 four-seamers among his 99 pitches regardless, 29 of them at 97 miles the hour or better and one at 99.4, the hardest of his career, across six scoreless innings in the longest postseason outing of his life; Tampa Bay's three runs, every one unearned, are manufactured from a walk, two infield choppers, an alert dash to an unguarded base and a ball that skips through José Ramírez's legs; and Parker Messick's boyhood-ballpark homecoming ends in a tough-luck defeat as the series packs for Cleveland tied at a game apiece

The evening's one secret was given away before the first pitch, and it kept perfectly well anyway. "The announcers before the game and even our PA were calling him 'Fastball Freddy,'" Kevin Cash grumbled afterward, half in jest. "That told everybody what was coming."4 What came, Tuesday night at Tropicana Field, was 71 four-seam fastballs among Freddy Peralta's 99 pitches — a reliance he had not permitted himself in any start since June of 2019 — and the forewarned Guardians went 3-for-17 against the pitch and never once scratched him.4 The figures read like an affidavit: 29 offerings at 97 miles the hour or better from a man whose season average was 94.3; a 99.4 to Jo Adell in the fifth, the hardest pitch of his nine-year career; 51 of the 71 heaters spotted at the top third of the strike zone or above it.43 "It's already an elite fastball, but he was placing it at the top for strikes," said Steven Kwan. "And then it felt like when he wanted to, he just put it a ball above. When he's doing that, it's pretty hard to lay off."4 Six scoreless innings — the longest postseason errand of Peralta's life — on four singles, two walks and a hit batsman, closed with a nine-pitch siege of Petey Halpin that ended in a changeup, a strikeout, a scream off the mound and the dome chanting "Freddy! Freddy!" at the Trade Deadline acquisition. His last eight starts, summer and October together, have now each allowed five hits or fewer and no more than one run, with a Tampa Bay victory to show for every one — the longest such run by any traditional starter since 1900.4

The three runs behind him were all unearned and all of a piece — "a very Rays inning," their own manager certified.6 Junior Caminero opened the fourth with a walk; Victor Mesa Jr.'s double-play bouncer was undone on review, the relay having pulled Nathaniel Lowe's foot from the bag; and after a strikeout, Chandler Simpson — making his first start since the second game of the Division round — chopped a ball five feet in front of the plate and outran the clean play. Mesa, observing that third base stood unguarded where Ramírez had drifted toward short, simply never stopped running.6 Then Ben Williamson beat a 2-1 changeup into the ground toward the surest glove in the league, and the ball struck the lip where the dirt meets the artificial turf, hopped off the top of Ramírez's mitt and passed between his legs into left field as Mesa trotted home.65 Liam Hicks, dropped to eighth in the order against the left hand, lined the next man's first pitch — a slider left up — to right-center for two more. One ball out of the infield in the whole rally, and the game decided by it. "They've done that all year," said Stephen Vogt. "When they smell blood, they take it and run."3

Cleveland's grief wants a careful accounting, for the club otherwise played a clean, hard game. Ramírez makes the play in question as near to always as the language allows; this once the bounce defeated him. "Nobody's perfect, but I still feel bad," the third baseman said through the club's interpreter. "The ball bounced right on the edge between the dirt and the turf. That's what made it more difficult for me."5 Kwan, who was himself victimized by the surface in the opener, offered the visiting fielder's lament: "It's kind of inconsistent whether it's going to hop or skip. When you don't play on it every day, you're just not calibrated to it."5 The offense supplied its own share, going 1-for-6 with runners in scoring position and leaving nine men aboard; the lone reply was Chase DeLauter's double to right in the seventh, cashing Patrick Bailey's walk.5 And Messick — whose homecoming to the ballpark of his boyhood this paper set out at length yesterday morning — deserved a kinder ledger than the one he signed: five innings, six hits, two walks, three runs and not one of them earned, a tough-luck defeat in the house he once watched from the cheap seats.5

The victors, it should be recorded, played the evening in fancy dress. Down a game, the Rays swapped into their Devil Rays throwbacks around ten o'clock that morning on a suggestion from the club's chief executive Ken Babby — a costume in which they had gone 12-3 during the regular season — and the swagger arrived with the wardrobe.7 Caminero leapt to spear Kwan's fifth-inning liner and administered a finger wag after the fashion of Dikembe Mutombo; by the seventh the two were conferring amiably at third base about it. "He told me, 'Hey, if I hit it a little bit harder, the ball's past you,'" Caminero reported. "And I said, 'Yeah, try to hit it harder and I won't catch it.'"7 So the 32,125 went home in two hours and forty-two minutes, and the round removes to the lakefront tied at one — no small adjustment of the odds, the home-field club having historically taken such a series 55 times in 102, and 24 of 40 in the pennant rounds. The third game goes Thursday evening at six o'clock Eastern at Progressive Field, and the Herald surveys that sitting elsewhere in this number.32

News Around the League

THE LINEUP DESK: THE QUESTION OF RESTING OHTANI IS ANSWERED BY THE MAN HIMSELF — 'ADAMANT' HE CAN HELP, THE GAME'S GREATEST INSTRUMENT TAKES HIS PLACE IN TONIGHT'S ORDER, MECHANICS, SYMPTOMS AND ALL

The conversation this paper reported yesterday has been held, and the player won it. Shohei Ohtani will bat for Los Angeles in tonight's third game, Dave Roberts announced Tuesday at Dodger Stadium, the club having weighed resting him and found the man immovable. "He was very convicted that he is onto something mechanically," the manager said. "He was adamant that he can help us. He's well enough to help us win a baseball game. So that's all I needed to hear."8 Roberts likened the sitting-down he did not order to the one he once gave Freddie Freeman, whose sprained ankle cost him three games of the 2024 postseason before five World Series appearances that entered legend.8

The figures that prompted the question have not improved for being aired. Ohtani stands at .197 with a .629 on-base-plus-slugging over his last 35 games, has not homered since August 18 — a drought of 110 plate appearances, the longest of his career — and is 3-for-20 this October without an extra-base hit, dropped from second in the order to cleanup. Speaking to the press for the first time since the eve of the Division round, he declined the alibi of the right biceps and left knee that have troubled him since June: "The symptoms shouldn't be the reason why I can't hit," he said through his interpreter.8 The remedies have been uncharacteristic — on-field batting practice four days running, from a man who takes it in public a handful of times a year, and even a show of bunt against a left-handed reliever on Monday.8 The opposition declines to read the ledger literally. "We remember vividly at this time last year that he maybe had the best baseball game ever played the day he pitched against us," said Milwaukee's Pat Murphy. "You can't forget that, his capabilities, whatever."8 On that much, every scorer in the press box agrees.

THE PRECIPICE DESK: TONIGHT AT EIGHT THE TWICE-CROWNED CHAMPIONS MAKE THEIR STAND AT HOME, TWO GAMES IN ARREARS — SNELL, WHO FACED THE MINIMUM THROUGH EIGHT AGAINST THESE SAME BREWERS A YEAR AGO, DRAWS THE ASSIGNMENT AGAINST GASSER, A MAN WHO BEGAN THIS SEASON IN NASHVILLE

The National League's argument resumes tonight at eight o'clock Eastern at Dodger Stadium, and the arithmetic of the precipice is plainly printed: clubs down two games to none in a best-of-seven have recovered the series 16 times in 95 trials, and of the 42 that ever fell behind three games to none, 32 were swept and exactly one — Roberts' own 2004 Red Sox, as the manager hardly needs reminding — climbed all the way out.9 "You want to get that first one," Roberts allows.9

His chosen instrument is the left hand with the best claim on Milwaukee's respect. Blake Snell, limited to nine starts this season by shoulder trouble and surgery on the elbow, was "too fine" by his manager's reckoning in his lone October outing, walking five men in an abbreviated Division-round start; but his five starts at Dodger Stadium this year show a 2.19 earned-run average, and his last acquaintance with these Brewers — in this very round, a year ago — ran eight scoreless innings in which he struck out ten and faced the minimum.910 "0-2, 2-0, it wouldn't matter," Snell said. "I know what I need to do to win and dominate." His teammate Teoscar Hernández counts the remaining cards without blinking: "We've got Snell, we've got Glasnow, and then we've got Tarik again... I think we're going to be OK."10

Milwaukee's answer is the season's quietest success story: Robert Gasser, who opened the year at Triple-A Nashville and enters a pennant-round start on a run of 2-0 with a 1.73 earned-run average over his last seven appearances — a rise that began in late August when a comebacker felled Dustin May on the game's first pitch and Gasser walked out of the bullpen into a rotation he has not left since.9 With Milwaukee's fourth-game starter yet unnamed, every inning the sweeper-artist supplies tonight is worth two. The home crowd, the probabilities and the champions' pride all report for duty at the same hour; the Herald will believe the obituaries when it sees the body.9

THE LAKEFRONT DESK: THE AMERICAN ROUND, NOW A BEST-OF-FIVE WITH THREE GAMES BY THE LAKE, RECONVENES THURSDAY AT SIX — JAX IS NAMED FOR TAMPA BAY, WILLIAMS STANDS LIKELY FOR CLEVELAND, AND THE LOUDEST YARD OF THE AUTUMN AWAITS THEM BOTH

The American League's pennant round rests today and reconvenes Thursday at six o'clock Eastern at Progressive Field, reduced by the split at the dome to a best-of-five in which Cleveland holds the next three home dates.112 The statisticians commend the appointment: in best-of-seven series knotted at one, the third game's winner has gone on to take the series 71 times in 102.5

Tampa Bay has named its man — Griffin Jax, a starter for most of the season, who carries a 0.90 earned-run average over his last five appearances and spent only 32 pitches in his lone Division-round errand, two tidy innings against the Yankees.11 Cleveland has named nobody, Vogt preferring to see how his staff emerges from the first two games, but the ball figures to belong to Gavin Williams on regular rest — the same Williams whose Division round ran to a 1.54 earned-run average with 24 strikeouts in 11 2/3 innings, closing one elimination game and starting the next.11

The venue is reckoned a combatant in its own right. The lakefront crowd that sang its club back from two games dead against Chicago now receives a series tied, and even the enemy tips his cap in advance. "That's as good an atmosphere as you're going to see," said Kevin Cash. "They've got a great fan base that's going to be behind their team."11 The marquee names, meanwhile, owe the round a signature: Ramírez's series so far holds one solid game and one costly error, and Caminero still awaits the first postseason home run of his career. One of the two clubs will put the sport's longest waits another game behind it Thursday — Cleveland's drought of 77 seasons against a Tampa Bay franchise that has never once, in 28 years, carried the flag home.11

THE MANAGERIAL DESK: SEATTLE ASKS LEAVE TO COURT THE MAN WHO KEPT HOUSTON'S MACHINE RUNNING — ESPADA, HIS CONTRACT EXPIRING WITH THE MONTH, WILL HEAR THE MARINERS OUT

Word from the executive corridors: Joe Espada, these past three seasons the manager of the Astros and for six before that their bench coach, will interview for Seattle's vacant managership, the Mariners having sought and received Houston's permission by the account of the wire's sources. Neither club confirms the courtship; the man's contract expires at the month's end, which rather confirms it for them.12

The résumé travels well. Espada's nine Houston years took in the 2022 championship, two further pennants and seven division titles, and his own three seasons at the helm ran 256-229 with the West's flag in 2024 and again this summer — though this summer's edition won it at 81-81 and was swept from the Wild Card round by the White Sox, a decline that had already cost the general manager Dana Brown his post in August.12 Espada, for his part, has said plainly he would like to continue in Houston.

Seattle's specification reads like a reply to its own history: the president of baseball operations Jerry Dipoto — whose two previous selections, Scott Servais and the departed Dan Wilson, had never managed a game at any level — now declares prior big-league experience "preferred" and the need to be for "fresh thought."12 A man with three division titles in three years, suddenly at liberty across the division, answers the advertisement almost suspiciously well. The Herald files the courtship under October's quieter competitions and will report the banns if they are published.12

A single game stands on tonight's card, and it may be the month's heaviest: the National League's third sitting, at eight o'clock Eastern at Dodger Stadium, where the champions of the last two World's Series stand twice beaten, with Snell on the hill and Ohtani batting on his own insistence. Thursday the calendar doubles again — Tampa Bay at Cleveland at six o'clock, Milwaukee at Los Angeles at nine.2 The week's two evenings at the dome have supplied a matched pair of lessons: Monday the form sheet burned, and Tuesday it was lovingly restored, the best fastball of a man's life and a single error punished to the last unearned run. The game gives and takes away with the same hand, and October keeps every receipt. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
